title: config/
description: Database, Redis, and Cloudinary setup.
text: database.js connects at import time and exits the process on failure — there is no retry. redis.js creates three lazy clients (presence, publish, subscribe) and stops retrying after five failures, letting the app run without Redis. cloudinary.js configures only when all three keys are present; otherwise uploads fall back to the local folder.

title: controllers/
description: Request handling, one module per area.
text: Controllers own the product rules: no self-connections, no duplicate requests, author-only deletes, poster-only application updates, messaging only between connections or active job pairs. Anything worth telling the user about goes through notifyUser, which stores the notification and emits it into the recipient room.

title: Entry point
description: App setup, route mounting, socket start, listen.
text: The entry requires the database connector (which connects on import), declares permissive CORS with credentials, serves uploads/ statically, answers /health and /api/health without auth or DB waits, mounts the API routers, hands the HTTP server to the socket initializer, and listens on PORT. trust proxy is set for rate limiting behind a proxy.

title: backend/
description: Express API plus the socket server, in one process.
text: One Node process serves HTTP and realtime together: index.js mounts the route modules, starts the socket server on the same HTTP server, and listens. Everything protected goes through the auth guard; uploads branch into Multer before reaching their controllers. Libraries used here: @socket.io/redis-adapter, Socket.io Redis adapter, bcryptjs, better-auth, cloudinary, Cloudinary, cookie-parser, cors, dotenv, express, Express, express-rate-limit, ioredis, jsonwebtoken, mongoose, Mongoose, multer, Multer, multer-storage-cloudinary, nodemailer, Nodemailer, socket.io, Socket.io, validator.

title: middleware/
description: Auth guard, rate limits, and upload handling.
text: The guard reads the jwt cookie first and falls back to the Authorization header — that fallback is what makes hosted frontends work where third-party cookies are blocked. Limits range from 15 auth attempts per 15 minutes to 60 searches per 5 minutes. Uploads pick Cloudinary storage when keys exist and local disk otherwise, cap files at 10MB, and convert Multer errors into 400 responses instead of crashes.

title: models/
description: Six Mongoose schemas, the database shape.
text: Messages, comments, and job applications are embedded subdocuments, not separate collections. Passwords hash on save with cost 12 and never leave the database (the field is excluded from queries by default). The chat model drops near-duplicate messages at save time and keeps the last-message timestamp fresh for conversation ordering.

title: routes/
description: One Express router per area, mounted under /api.
text: All routers except contact apply the auth guard; register, login, logout, and the contact form stay public. Auth, connection, search, post, and job routes carry rate limits. Avatar, cover, post-image, and document uploads attach Multer middleware for their single field before the controller runs.

title: utils/
description: The Socket.io server.
text: One file owns realtime end to end. Sockets register a user id and join that id as a room, so any process can reach a user by id once the Redis adapter is attached. Presence is tracked twice: a local socket map for instant lookups and a Redis hash so other instances agree. Typing and status broadcasts are never stored; messages always are, with sent, delivered, and read states.

title: Hosting notes
description: What vercel.json configures, and the Socket.io caveat.
headings: Can Socket.io run in that setup?
text: Two config files, two different jobs: The **root vercel.json** uses the legacy builds/routes syntax to run backend/index.js as a Node function and route every path to it. It says nothing about the frontend. **frontend/vercel.json** is a single SPA rewrite: any path without a dot serves /, so React Router owns deep links. Neither file provisions MongoDB, Redis, Cloudinary, or mail — those stay external services with environment variables. Can Socket.io run in that setup? Honestly: only with caveats. Vercel Functions serve WebSocket connections (Public Beta since June 2026, last verified 2026-10-11), and Socket.IO is listed as supported — but connections are pinned to one function instance up to its maximum duration, reconnects may land on a different instance, and clients must handle reconnects. The repo's Redis adapter is exactly the right shock absorber for that world, and the socket client already reconnects with backoff. The code comments also reference Render (uptime-ping health endpoints, proxy trust, cross-site cookie notes), so the author has clearly run the backend on a long-lived host too. This project does not claim where the author hosts DevConnect, and the legacy builds syntax in the root config predates the current functions-based configuration style. Last verified 2026-10-11. Official references: WebSockets on Vercel Functions Do Vercel Serverless Functions support WebSocket connections? Socket.IO troubleshooting on serverless

title: Deployment overview
description: What has to run for DevConnect to work.
text: DevConnect needs four external services, two of them optional with degradation: **MongoDB** (required) — every collection lives here. The backend exits on a failed connection; there is no retry. **Redis** (optional, degrades) — presence hash and the Socket.io adapter. Without it, realtime works on a single instance only. **Cloudinary** (optional, degrades) — image and document storage. Without keys, uploads land in the backend uploads/ folder and are served statically by Express. **Email over Gmail SMTP** (optional, degrades) — the contact form answers 503 without credentials. The backend is one long-lived Node process serving HTTP and sockets from the same port; the frontend is a static Vite build talking to it over REST plus sockets. See Environment variables for the full table and Hosting notes for what the repo's vercel.json files actually configure. Last verified against the documented commit on 2026-10-11. This project makes no claim about where the author hosts it.

title: Authentication
description: Email register and login plus GitHub OAuth, on JWT.
text: Authentication is JWT plus bcrypt — better-auth sits in both manifests but no source file imports it. Email users register and log in through the user controller with 30-day tokens; GitHub users arrive through OAuth and get the same token. The guard reads the cookie first and the Bearer header second, which keeps hosted frontends working. One honest gap: the signup page reads a fulfilled matcher off a plain thunk, so its post-submit redirect is unverified — login and session restore follow the same token path and are straightforward.

title: Connections
description: Requests, accepts, lists, and removal.
text: One row per pair, unique on the ordered pair, with a pending, accepted, or rejected state. Sending notifies the recipient; accepting notifies the requester; rejecting only flips the state. Lists return the *other* user, populated for display. Accepted connections are the main gate for chat.

title: Feed and posts
description: Publishing, feed, likes, and comments.
text: Posts carry text, an optional image URL, a code snippet with language, a type, tags, and a collaboration flag. The recent tab pages by cursor; the top tab aggregates like counts over the last week. Code snippets render with syntax highlighting in the post card. Likes and comments both notify the post author.

title: Features
description: What DevConnect does, one page per feature.
text: Seven features, each with a slice diagram from page to model: Authentication Profiles and uploads Connections Feed and posts Jobs Notifications Real-time chat

title: Jobs
description: Listings, resume applications, and status tracking.
text: List views strip applications down to counts and an applied flag; only the poster sees full applications on the detail view. Applying attaches a resume plus up to five extra documents through the document uploader and notifies the poster. Active job pairs (poster plus pending, reviewed, or accepted applicants) may message each other without a connection.

title: Notifications
description: Stored rows plus live pushes, one helper.
text: Every notification is a stored row first — connection requests and accepts, likes, comments, job applications, and new messages — so nothing is lost when the recipient is offline. The same helper then pushes into the recipient room for instant display. Self-actions never notify. The bell catches up over REST with unread counts; live arrivals land through the socket service into the slice.

title: Profiles and uploads
description: Editable profiles with avatar and cover uploads.
text: Profiles mix hand-written fields with synced GitHub data (stats, top repos, skills derived from repo languages). Avatar and cover uploads ride the same Multer-plus-Cloudinary path as post images, with a local fallback. Discovery has two doors: the paged user feed (excluding the user and their connections) and name-or-skill search.

title: Real-time chat
description: Rooms, messages, receipts, typing, and presence.
text: Chat has two doors that stay in sync: socket events for live exchange and REST for history and sending from cold state. Every message is stored with a delivery state — sent when the peer is offline, delivered when present, read when the thread opens. Typing and presence are ephemeral broadcasts; only chat content is durable. The Redis adapter lets any instance reach any user room, so the design survives more than one server.

title: Folder structure
description: Where everything lives and why.
text: Two apps, each with its own layout. The backend groups by technical role — config/, routes/, controllers/, models/, middleware/, utils/ — with the entry file at the root. The frontend groups by UI role — pages/, components/, services/, store/, hooks/, lib/, utils/ — with App.jsx and main.jsx at the src/ root. Uploads and helper scripts (fix_db.js, test-cloudinary.js, dummy.txt) exist in the backend folder without being part of the architecture — the backend pages name them but do not document their contents.

title: Backend on Render
description: HTTP service, WebSocket service, and flush worker as Render services.
text: All three backend services build with tsc -b and start with node dist/index.js. Only Web Service, Postgres, Key Value, and static sites support free instances, so on the free tier every service here is a Render web service — the background-worker service type is paid-only. **Deploy the HTTP service.** Build tsc -b, start node dist/index.js, listening port from PORT (default 5000). It exposes /health, which is also the keep-alive target. Give it DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, and the auth, origin, ticket, email, and OAuth variables from the environment page. **Deploy the WebSocket service.** Build tsc -b, start node dist/index.js, listening port from WS_PORT (default 8080, a separate variable from PORT). It answers only WebSocket upgrades and exposes no HTTP route. Give it DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, PRESENCE_TICKET_SECRET (must match the HTTP service), WEB_ORIGIN, and WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. **Deploy the flush worker as an always-on service.** Same build and start commands. It runs a continuous BullMQ process against DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL, so it needs paid uptime — pinging cannot run it (see the keep-alive page). Without it, room state stays in Redis and snapshots never become durable revisions. Last verified: 2026-10-11. Free-tier limits change — check the providers before relying on any number. title: Cold starts and keep-alive
description: Why free services sleep, the hours math, and how to ping them awake.
headings: Option 1: Cloudflare Worker with a Cron Trigger
text: Render spins a free web service down after 15 minutes without inbound traffic, and waking takes roughly a minute. Each workspace gets 750 free instance hours a month, shared by all free web services; spun-down services use no hours, and exceeding the allowance suspends every free service until next month. Render may also restart a free service at any time. The hours math Hours equal services times hours per day times days: | Services awake | Hours/day | Days | Hours/month | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 2 | 24 | 31 | ~1,488 — over the 750 limit | | 1 | 24 | 31 | ~744 — leaves nothing for others | | 2 | 8 | 30 | ~480 — fits with room to spare | Keeping both services awake around the clock is not possible on free. Ping only inside a daily window instead — 8 hours a day for both services costs about 480 hours a month. Ping every 10 minutes, which sits safely under the 15-minute idle limit. Never ping /robots.txt: while a service is spun down, Render answers that path itself and the service never wakes. Target the HTTP service's /health. For the WS service, ping its public HTTP URL — but know what it does: the WS server answers only WebSocket upgrades, so a plain GET gets no application response (checked against the code with a local bare-server test). The inbound connection still counts as traffic; confirm the service really stays awake in the Render dashboard during your window. Option 1: Cloudflare Worker with a Cron Trigger Free and precise. The Worker fetches both URLs on a schedule; both URLs come from env vars. **Convert the window to UTC.** Cron Triggers run in UTC. Subtract your offset from both ends of your 8-hour window — 08:00–16:00 at UTC+2 becomes 06:00–14:00 UTC, written as */10 6-13 * *. Half-hour zones should round the window out to whole hours, and zones with daylight saving need the cron adjusted twice a year. **Deploy with Wrangler and check the first runs.** Trigger changes can take several minutes to propagate. title: Database and Redis
description: Neon Postgres, Upstash Redis, then run the migrations.
text: Postgres is the durable authority and Redis the live one, so give each a managed home: a Neon Postgres database and an Upstash Redis database, both reachable over their TCP connection strings. Do not use Render's free Key Value for rooms — it keeps state in memory only and loses everything on restart. **Create the Neon database and copy its connection string.** It becomes DATABASE_URL for every backend service. The database client throws without it. **Create the Upstash Redis database and copy its connection string.** It becomes REDIS_URL for every backend service. Use the TCP URL, not an HTTP one. **Run the migrations from packages/db.** Run db:emit, then db:migration-check, then db:migrate for a fresh database. For an existing database, verify migration and schema state first instead of resetting it. Last verified: 2026-10-11. Free-tier limits change — check the providers before relying on any number. title: Verify and troubleshoot
description: Deployment checks first, then fixes for what usually breaks.
text: Deployment checks **Migrations applied.** db:migrate ran clean against the Neon database from packages/db. **HTTP service answers.** Its public /health URL returns a response, and the scenes API works behind authentication. **WebSocket service upgrades.** A room page connects, presence appears, and commits reconcile across two tabs. **Flush worker running.** Room edits become durable scene revisions in Postgres — not just Redis state. **Web app wired.** The deployed editor points at the deployed API and WebSocket URLs, and sign-in plus invites work end to end. Troubleshooting | Symptom | Likely cause and fix | | --- | --- | | First request slow | Cold start — the service was spun down and takes about a minute to wake. title: Installation

text: You need Node.js 24+, pnpm 11.25.0, PostgreSQL 15+, and Redis. Email delivery is needed for verification and invites; Google OAuth is optional. By default the editor runs on port 3000 (with the dashboard on the same port), the HTTP API on port 5000, the WebSocket server on port 8080, and Redis on port 6379.

title: Auth

text: Signing in is email-based with verification links; Google OAuth is optional. Rooms never take a password or a session cookie over the socket: the HTTP server issues a short-lived presence ticket, and the WebSocket server verifies it during the upgrade before checking room access. title: Backend common
description: Server-only collaboration and access operations shared by HTTP, WebSocket, and worker apps.
text: There is exactly one write path for room data, and all three backend services use it: the commit is checked against the caller's role, replayed mutations are dropped, the batch is validated and reconciled, and the result lands in the live store, falling back to the database when Redis is unavailable. Libraries used here: dotenv, @types/node, vitest, Vitest.

title: Common
description: Platform-neutral element models, collaboration protocols, validation, and reconciliation.
text: Room commits reconcile deterministically per element: both sides apply the same winner-picking rules, so concurrent edits converge without a central lock. The protocol caps everything it carries — elements per commit, preview sizes, selection ids — and the validators enforce those caps on both ends of the socket. Libraries used here: vitest, Vitest.

title: Database
description: The sole Prisma schema, database client, repositories, migration graph, and schema snapshots.
text: Durable room state is a versioned chain of scene revisions, each stamped with its actor. The flush worker appends new revisions only when the stored head is behind and prunes everything but the latest ones. Servers enforce owner, editor, and viewer permissions on every access. Libraries used here: @prisma/orm-postgres, Prisma ORM, dotenv, pg, node-postgres, @prisma/cli-engine, Prisma CLI engine, @types/node, @types/pg, prisma, Prisma CLI, tsx, typescript, TypeScript.

title: Engine
description: Browser-independent drawing geometry, tools, renderer, scene capture, and history.
text: The engine never touches the network or the DOM data layer: tools produce geometry, the scene keeps state and history, and the renderer turns state into sketch-style paths with a seeded randomizer so strokes look hand-drawn but render identically. Frames stay flat and axis-aligned by construction. Libraries used here: vitest, Vitest.

title: Redis
description: Redis live room state, pub/sub, rate limiting, and write-behind queue integration.
text: Redis is the live authority and Postgres the durable one. Snapshot writes are atomic with a Lua version check; when a write lands, the room joins the dirty set and a coalesced flush job is scheduled — debounced, with a maximum wait, and forced when the last participant leaves. Rate budgets are per connection for ephemeral frames and stricter for commits. Libraries used here: bullmq, BullMQ, ioredis, @types/node, tsx, typescript, TypeScript.

title: Reminders
description: Local scheduled notifications, reconciled.
text: All reminders are local and scheduled — no push service exists. Times and OS identifiers persist in SQLite; the reconcile pass schedules what is missing and drops what is stale whenever data, accounts, or sync change. description: Consistency math over local entries.
text: Consistency counts scheduled check-ins completed through the current day — future days never dilute the score. Best weekday looks back thirty days. Per-habit screens reuse the same summaries with their own history view.

title: features/tasks

title: Arrays and array methods
description: map, filter, reduce, find, the sort pitfall, and mutating versus new.
text: Array methods encode intent: map transforms, filter selects, reduce folds. Interviewers ask this to hear you pick by return shape — and to catch the in-place sort corrupting shared state. Real-life situation A dashboard lists orders over $50 with their revenue total. filter picks the big orders, map pulls their totals, reduce folds one revenue number — three readable steps, no manual loop, original array untouched. Then a sort for the leaderboard mutates the shared ranks array, and every other widget shows the new order too. Visual Try it const orders = [ id: 1, total: 30 , id: 2, total: 120 , id: 3, total: 80 , ]; const big = orders.filter(function (o) return o.total >= 50; ); console.log(big.length); const sums = big.map(function (o) return o.total; ); console.log(sums[0]); console.log(sums[1]); const revenue = sums.reduce(function (sum, n) return sum + n; , 0); console.log(revenue); const ranks = [10, 9, 80]; console.log(ranks.sort()[0]); console.log( ranks.slice().sort(function (a, b) return a - b; )[0], ); Try changing the filter to o.total > 100 and predict the revenue first. Then sort a copy with toSorted and compare. Time yourself rewriting the pipeline with a single reduce, then compare readability honestly. Mutating versus new Chain the non-mutating ones (map, filter, slice, toSorted) for shared data. Reserve sort, splice and reverse for local scratch arrays nobody else sees. const bids = [10, 9, 80]; console.log(bids.sort()[0]); Key takeaways map/filter return new arrays; reduce folds to one value. Default sort is lexicographic and in place — pass a comparator, copy first. Pick methods by return shape: transform, select, find or fold. References Array reference. sort comparator. title: async/await and error handling
description: Straight-line async code, try/catch, and the parallel patterns.
headings: When await helps, when it hurts
text: async/await writes asynchronous code that reads top-to-bottom: awaits for sequencing, try/catch for errors. Interviewers ask this because the syntax looks synchronous while the pitfalls (serial loops, uncaught rejections, fire-and-forget) are anything but. Real-life situation A settings save retries a flaky endpoint with backoff: try, wait a little longer each time, give up after three attempts with a real error. Written with await, the retry loop reads like its flowchart. Written with nested callbacks, the same logic hides behind three indent levels. Visual Try it async function fetchWithRetry(url, tries) let attempt = 0; while (attempt Try dropping tries to 2 and watch it give up. Then retry /missing and explain why backoff never saves a 404. When await helps, when it hurts Await for sequencing and error handling. Never await independent calls one by one — launch them all, gather once. And never fire-and-forget an async call in reviewed code: return it or catch it. async function run() const out = []; for (const n of [1, 2]) out.push(await Promise.resolve(n * 2)); return out; run().then(function (out) console.log(out[0] + "," + out[1]); ); Key takeaways async wraps returns in promises; await parks only its function. Rejected awaits throw at that line — guard with try/catch. Launch independent work together; gather with all or allSettled`. References async function. await operator. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Call stack and execution context
description: Frames, push and pop, overflow, and reading a trace.
text: Every call pushes a frame — its variables plus where to resume — and every return pops it. Interviewers ask this because "Maximum call stack size exceeded" and frozen pages both start here, and reading a trace starts here too. Real-life situation A receipt printer recurses into bundled items, but a bundle containing itself loops forever and the tab dies with a stack overflow. The trace shows the same function repeated — the giveaway. The fix is a visited set plus an iterative fallback, but noticing the repeated frame is the interview skill. Visual Try it function factorial(n) console.log("enter " + n); if (n Try raising the factorial input until the runner stops you, and read which error names the stack. Then trace the leave lines back to their frames. When depth matters Recursion fits nested data (trees, comments, DOM walks). Flat sequences want loops, and unbounded depth wants chunking so frames pop between batches. Depth is always bounded — engines don't do tail-call optimization. function a() console.log("a-start"); b(); console.log("a-end"); function b() console.log("b"); a();` Key takeaways Calls push frames; returns pop them; last in, first out. Overflow means calls outrun returns — find the missing base case. Read traces top-down: the thrower first, your code a few frames down. References Call stack (MDN glossary). Recursion guide. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Callbacks and callback hell
description: Error-first callbacks, nesting, and the escapes that actually work.
text: A callback is a function you hand over to run later — and nesting them turns error handling into a rightward pyramid. Interviewers ask this because the pyramid is style, but the trust problem underneath (called once? called ever?) is why promises exist. Real-life situation A profile page loads the user, then their orders, with error handling at each step. Nested inline, the happy path drifts right and every level repeats its guard. Named functions flatten it back — and promisifying ends the nesting for good. Seen in: Express 4 error middleware receives errors through next(err), the error-first convention at framework scale (Express 4, 2014, error handling). Visual Try it function readUser(id, done) setTimeout(function () done(null, id: id, name: "ada" ); , 5); function readOrders(user, done) setTimeout(function () done(null, ["book", "pen"]); , 5); readUser(1, function (error, user) if (error) console.log("user failed"); return; readOrders(user, function (err, orders) if (err) console.log("orders failed"); return; console.log(user.name + ":" + orders.length); ); ); Try deleting the if (error) guard and passing a failing reader — watch the crash move somewhere unhelpful. Then extract both inline callbacks into named functions and feel the pyramid flatten. When callbacks still win Single-shot "when" events with no failure mode: listeners, timers, array iteration. Callbacks for events, promises for operations — and convert at the boundary with a wrapper instead of mixing both in one flow. function load(done) done(new Error("offline")); load(function (error, data) if (error) console.log("caught"); return; console.log(data); ); Key takeaways Callbacks hand control to someone else: called once, ever, with what args? Error-first means (err, data) with an early bail on err. Flatten with named functions; escape with promises and await. References Callbacks (MDN glossary). Express error handling. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Closures
description: Functions that remember their scope, private state, and the loop bug.
text: A closure is a function bundled with the variables around it at creation. It is the most-asked JavaScript interview topic because it explains private state, callbacks and half of all async bugs in one mechanism. Real-life situation Two shopping carts on one page must not share items. A cart factory returns add and count functions closing over a private items array — each cart gets its own scope, so adding to one never touches the other. No classes, no naming tricks; the scope boundary is the privacy boundary. Seen in: React's useState closes over each render's scope, which is why late-running callbacks can see stale values (React 16.8, 2019, useState reference). Visual Try it function createCart() const items = []; return add: function (item) items.push(item); , count: function () return items.length; , ; const first = createCart(); const second = createCart(); first.add("book"); first.add("pen"); console.log(first.count()); console.log(second.count()); function counter() let n = 0; return function () n = n + 1; return n; ; const next = counter(); console.log(next()); console.log(next()); Try adding a third cart and sharing one items array between two factories — watch independence break. Then convert counter to an object with reset. Each render in UI code closes over its own props the same way, which is why stale values surprise even experienced developers. for (var i = 0; i Key takeaways Closures link live variables, not snapshots. Factory + closure is the simplest private state in the language. Shared loop bindings (var) are the classic closure bug; let` fixes it. References Closures guide. let and block scope. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Data types and type coercion
description: typeof quirks, null versus undefined, NaN, equality, and truthy traps.
headings: When to convert, when to compare
text: JavaScript converts types behind your back in exactly the spots where money and access checks live. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can predict an expression's value — and defend user input against silent conversion. Real-life situation A cart form sends price and quantity as strings. "4" + 2 totals "42" instead of 6, and the order goes through overcharged. The fix is boring on purpose: convert with Number() at the boundary, reject NaN, and compare with === so types can never sneak past. Visual Try it function cartTotal(price, quantity) return price + quantity; console.log(cartTotal("4", 2)); console.log(cartTotal(4, 2)); function safeTotal(price, quantity) const cleanPrice = Number(price); const cleanQuantity = Number(quantity); if (Number.isNaN(cleanPrice)) return "bad price"; if (Number.isNaN(cleanQuantity)) return "bad quantity"; return cleanPrice + cleanQuantity; console.log(safeTotal("4", 2)); console.log(safeTotal("four", 2)); console.log(safeTotal(4, 0)); Try changing the last call to safeTotal(4, "") and explain why the result is 4, not "bad quantity". Then try safeTotal(0, 0). Log typeof every value crossing a form boundary for a week; the habit pays for itself. When to convert, when to compare Convert at boundaries (forms, URLs, storage) with Number() or String() and nowhere else. Compare with === always; reach for == never. When 0 or "" are valid values, default with ??, not ||. console.log(0 == ""); console.log(0 === ""); console.log(null == undefined); Key takeaways + concatenates when either side is a string; convert inputs first. === compares type and value; == converts and surprises. Eight falsy values exist; empty arrays and objects are truthy. References Equality comparisons. typeof operator. Truthy and falsy. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: The DOM and events
description: Capturing, bubbling, delegation, and safe dynamic lists.
headings: When to delegate, when to bind directly
text: Events travel down to their target and bubble back up — and one parent listener using that bubble beats a hundred individual ones. Interviewers ask this because delegation, propagation control and dynamic rows are daily DOM work. Real-life situation A to-do list adds rows all day. Binding each row's button misses every future row, so deletes silently stop working after the first add. One listener on the list, reading event.target.closest("li"), handles present and future rows alike — try it live below, including the add button. Seen in: jQuery's .on() unified direct and delegated binding this way (jQuery 1.7, 2011, on() docs). Visual Try it task 0 done add task left: 1 ' const list = document.querySelector("#todo"); const status = document.querySelector("#status"); let added = 0; list.addEventListener("click", function (event) const item = event.target.closest("li"); if (!item) return; item.remove(); status.textContent = "left: " + list.children.length; ); document.querySelector("#add").addEventListener("click", function () added = added + 1; const item = document.createElement("li"); item.textContent = "task " + added; const remove = document.createElement("button"); remove.textContent = "done"; item.appendChild(remove); list.appendChild(item); ); console.log("ready:" + list.children.length); Click a done button, then add a task and delete it too — no new listeners were ever bound. Then try removing the closest line and click the list padding to see why the guard matters. When to delegate, when to bind directly Delegate dynamic lists and repeated controls from a stable parent. Bind directly for one-off controls with no future siblings. Stop propagation only when ancestors must not react; prevent default to cancel the browser action. console.log(typeof document); Key takeaways Events capture down, then bubble up; listeners default to bubbling. Delegate from stable parents; read event.target, anchor currentTarget. textContent for user strings; innerHTML only for stat

title: The event loop
description: The flagship page — stack, queues, and the order everything runs in.
text: One thread runs your code; everything slow waits in queues, and the loop feeds them onto the stack when it's free. This page is the most-asked JavaScript interview topic because the sync-timer-promise order puzzle appears in screens, onsites and take-homes alike. Real-life situation A dashboard logs "loading", fires a data fetch, schedules a refresh timer and logs "ready". Users report the timer beating the data although both were "immediate". The cause is queue priority, not speed: the promise reaction drains as a microtask right after the script, while the zero-delay timer waits a full loop turn. Knowing the order turns a mystery into a schedule. Seen in: Node.js documents its loop phases, timers and nextTick ordering in the official event loop guide (Node.js, 2009, event loop guide). Visual Try it console.log("script start"); setTimeout(function () console.log("timer"); , 0); Promise.resolve().then(function () console.log("promise"); ); console.log("script end"); async function load() console.log("load start"); await sleep(10); console.log("load done"); load(); console.log("after call"); // Timers wait a full turn; promises drain first. Try changing the timer delay to 20 and predict before running. Then move the promise below load() and check the order holds. Browser versus Node, briefly Browsers add a render step per turn; Node runs timer, I/O and check phases per iteration. Both drain microtasks the same way. Node-only extras: process.nextTick (before even promises) and setImmediate (next check phase). Same mental model, different machinery. console.log("a"); setTimeout(function () console.log("b"); , 0); Promise.resolve().then(function () console.log("c"); ); Key takeaways Sync runs first, microtasks drain completely, then one task per turn. Zero-delay timers still wait a full turn; promises don't. await parks the function, never the thread. References Event loop guide (Node). Concurrency model (MDN). HTML event loops. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Fetch, CORS and browser storage
description: Await-await-ok, CORS in practice, and cookies versus storages.
text: fetch resolves on HTTP errors, browsers gate cross-origin reads, and storage is strings-only — three facts that decide whether data code works. Interviewers ask this because "await, await, ok" plus a CORS explanation covers most real data bugs. Real-life situation A profile loader awaits the user, then the avatar, then renders — but a 404 renders as a broken page instead of "user missing", because fetch never rejected. Checking res.ok turns the silent bad render into a handled empty state. Meanwhile a search box aborts its previous request on every keystroke, so slow replies can't overwrite fresh ones. Visual Try it async function loadUser(id) const res = await fakeFetch("/users/" + id, latencyMs: 5 ); if (!res.ok) return "user missing:" + res.status; const user = await res.json(); return user.name; console.log(await loadUser(1)); console.log(await loadUser(99)); async function loadAbort() const controller = new AbortController(); const pending = fakeFetch("/users", latencyMs: 50, signal: controller.signal, ); controller.abort(); try await pending; return "arrived"; catch (error) return error.name; console.log(await loadAbort()); Try pointing the first call at /flaky and watch it throw instead of returning. Then give loadAbort no abort and confirm "arrived". function saveDraft(text) return JSON.stringify( text: text ); function loadDraft(raw) try return JSON.parse(raw).text; catch (error) return "empty"; const raw = saveDraft("hi"); console.log(loadDraft(raw)); console.log(loadDraft("###")); console.log(loadDraft(null)); Cookies versus storages Cookies travel with every request (sessions, auth flags) and hide behind HttpOnly. localStorage persists per origin without traveling (themes, drafts). sessionStorage dies with the tab (wizard state). Secrets go in HttpOnly cookies, never in readable storage — one paragraph on XSS: build markup only from trusted strings, or attacker text becomes your code. async function status(id) const res = await fakeFetch("/users/" + id,

title: Functions
description: Declarations, expressions, arrows, callbacks and higher-order functions.
text: Functions are values you can store, pass and return — that single idea powers callbacks, array methods and most libraries. Interviewers ask this to see whether you reach for the right shape: declaration, expression or arrow. Real-life situation A login form needs three checks: email shape, password length, and both together. Writing each check as a small function and combining them with a higher-order validator keeps every rule testable alone — and the "validate everything" line reads like the requirement itself. Visual Try it function isEmail(value) return value.includes("@") && value.includes("."); const isLongEnough = function (value) return value.length >= 8; ; const checkPassword = (value) => isLongEnough(value); function validate(fields, checks) return checks.map(function (check) return check(fields); ); const form = email: "ada@example.com", password: "s3cret!!" ; const results = validate(form, [ function (f) return isEmail(f.email); , function (f) return checkPassword(f.password); , ]); console.log(results[0]); console.log(results[1]); console.log(results.every(Boolean)); Try changing the arrow checkPassword to a function expression — same result. Then make the password "short" and watch which line flips. Finally, wrap one check so it runs only once and notice how much state even a tiny reusable wrapper needs. When to use which Declarations for standalone helpers (hoisted, mockable). Expressions and arrows for callbacks passed inline. Arrows when you want the outer this; function when the caller must set this. function applyTwice(fn, value) return fn(fn(value)); console.log( applyTwice(function (n) return n + 1; , 5), ); Key takeaways Declarations hoist; expressions and arrows must be defined first. Arrows inherit this; function receives it from the call. Higher-order functions take or return functions to reuse behavior. References Functions guide. Arrow functions. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: How JavaScript works
description: Engine and runtime, one thread, JIT in a paragraph, browser versus Node.
headings: The engine: turn text into speed
The runtime: everything around the engine
text: Your code runs inside two cooperating systems: the engine executes it and the runtime schedules everything around it. Interviewers ask this to check whether "single-threaded" and "asynchronous" fit together in your head. The engine: turn text into speed The engine parses your source into a tree, compiles the hot paths to machine code while the program runs, and re-optimizes as it learns. That compile-while-running trick is called just-in-time (JIT) compilation: the first run is quick to start, the thousandth loop is genuinely fast, and the engine quietly de-optimizes when one of its guesses proves wrong. The runtime: everything around the engine The engine alone can't wait, draw or fetch. The runtime adds the call stack (one thread doing one thing), the heap (where objects live), task and microtask queues (where callbacks wait), and the host APIs (timers, network, DOM). The event loop — the scheduler from the next pages — moves callbacks from queues onto the stack when it is free. Browser versus Node | | Browser | Node.js | |---|---|---| | Host APIs | DOM, fetch, timers, storage | Files, sockets, processes, timers | | Rendering | Yes, paints the page | No screen at all | | Extra queues | Render steps | process.nextTick, immediates | | Modules | ES modules, import maps | ES modules and CommonJS | Same language and same loop idea; different surroundings. Timer and promise code behaves the same in both until you touch host-specific APIs. Last verified: 2026-10-12. Key takeaways The engine runs code; the runtime schedules waiting, drawing and fetching. One thread runs your code; everything slow is delegated and called back. Browser and Node share the language but offer different host APIs. References How JavaScript works (MDN). V8 engine docs. The Node.js event loop.

title: Memory and garbage collection
description: Reachability, the three classic leaks, and matching teardowns.
text: JavaScript frees what you can't reach and keeps everything else — so memory management is reference management. Interviewers ask this because the three classic leaks (timers, detached DOM, growing caches) all reduce to one forgotten reference. Real-life situation A dashboard caches every view it opens "for speed" and never prunes. After an hour the tab crawls: each cached view is still reachable, so the collector can't free a byte. The fix is a matching teardown — cap the cache, clear it on logout — the same discipline as clearing timers and removing listeners. Visual Try it const cache = []; function remember(view) cache.push(view); function openView(name) const view = name: name, data: [1, 2, 3] ; remember(view); return view.name; console.log(openView("home")); console.log(openView("search")); console.log(cache.length); cache.length = 0; console.log(cache.length); const listeners = []; function onEvent(handler) listeners.push(handler); onEvent(function () return "click"; ); onEvent(function () return "hover"; ); console.log(listeners.length); listeners.length = 0; console.log(listeners.length); Try commenting out cache.length = 0 and watch the count stick. Then give remember a size cap that drops the oldest view past five entries. When it applies Any long-lived page: dashboards, editors, chats. Short-lived scripts rarely leak enough to matter — but the teardown habit (every setup gets an undo) pays off in components, where mount/unmount repeats the cycle constantly. function subscribe() const big = [1, 2, 3]; return function () return big.length; ; const read = subscribe(); console.log(read()); Key takeaways Reachable survives; unreachable is freed — leaks are forgotten references. The big three: stray timers, detached DOM, unbounded caches. Every setup needs a teardown on the same lifecycle. References Memory management (MDN). Heap snapshots (Chrome DevTools). title: Objects, prototypes and classes
description: Lookup chains, new, and classes as syntax over prototypes.
headings: When classes help, when they hide
text: Objects inherit through a chain: a missing key is looked up on the prototype, then its prototype, until null. Interviewers ask this because "shared methods, own data" explains classes, instanceof and half of all framework code. Real-life situation A device settings page builds phones and laptops from one Device constructor. The info method lives once on the prototype, so a thousand devices share one function while each keeps its own name. A Laptop subclass reuses the wiring through extends without copying anything. Visual Try it function Device(name) this.name = name; Device.prototype.info = function () return "device:" + this.name; ; const phone = new Device("pixel"); console.log(phone.info()); console.log(phone.hasOwnProperty("info")); class Laptop extends Device constructor(name, ram) super(name); this.ram = ram; const notebook = new Laptop("thinkpad", 16); console.log(notebook.info()); console.log(notebook instanceof Device); console.log(notebook instanceof Laptop); Try adding phone.info = "mine" and watch hasOwnProperty flip while the prototype stays shared. Then check notebook.hasOwnProperty("ram"). Sketch the three-box chain for your example on paper once — lookup questions get easy when you can see the links. When classes help, when they hide Classes help for instance hierarchies with shared behavior (devices, views, errors). They hide when a factory plus closures would do — prefer the simpler shape until inheritance earns its keep. const base = role: "user" ; const admin = Object.create(base); admin.role = "admin"; console.log(admin.role); console.log(base.role); Key takeaways Missing keys walk the prototype chain to null. new makes an object, links it, runs the constructor with this, returns it. Classes are constructors plus prototypes with safer defaults. References Prototype chain. Classes reference. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Performance patterns
description: Debounce, throttle, memoization — and doing less, less often.
text: Fast pages are rarely clever algorithms; they are fewer handlers, fewer renders, fewer requests. Interviewers ask this because debounce/throttle/ memoize are three memorizable shapes that fix entire classes of jank. Real-life situation A search box fetches on every keystroke — ten requests for "javascript", nine of them wasted, the slowest winning. Debouncing to 300ms of silence fires once with the final text. The scroll feed beside it uses throttle instead: position checks at most every 100ms while scrolling continues. Seen in: Lodash ships battle-tested debounce and throttle with cancel, flush and leading/trailing options (Lodash, 2012, debounce docs). Visual Try it function debounce(fn, wait) let timer = null; return function () const args = arguments; const self = this; clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(function () fn.apply(self, args); , wait); ; let searches = 0; const search = debounce(function (q) searches = searches + 1; , 20); search("t"); search("te"); search("tea"); await sleep(60); console.log(searches); Try dropping the clearTimeout line and count the calls. Then add a cancel method on the returned function that clears the timer. When each applies Debounce bursty, restartable work (search, resize, autosave). Throttle continuous feedback (scroll, mousemove). Memoize pure, expensive, repeated calls — and cap the cache before it becomes the leak. Otherwise: delegate, bail early, render less. function memoize(fn) const cache = ; return function (key) if (!(key in cache)) cache[key] = fn(key); return cache[key]; ; let calls = 0; const price = memoize(function (id) calls = calls + 1; return id * 10; ); console.log(price(2)); console.log(price(2)); console.log(calls); Key takeaways Debounce waits for silence; throttle meters a steady drip. Memoize pure repeated calls; cap the cache. Cheapest wins are structural: delegate, bail early, render less. References Debounce and throttle patterns. Lodash debounce. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Promises
description: States, chaining, error flow, and the four combinators.
text: A promise is a value with a schedule: pending now, settled exactly once later. Interviewers ask this because chains encode sequencing, error flow and parallelism — the three async skills — in one uniform shape. Real-life situation A dashboard needs the user and their posts before first paint. Fired together and joined with Promise.all, one wait covers both, results stay ordered, and a single .catch guards the whole load. Fired in sequence with separate awaits, the same dashboard takes twice as long for no reason. Visual Try it function getUser() return fakeFetch("/users/1", latencyMs: 5 ); function getPosts() return fakeFetch("/posts?userId=1", latencyMs: 5 ); Promise.all([getUser(), getPosts()]) .then(function (responses) return Promise.all( responses.map(function (r) return r.json(); ), ); ) .then(function (parts) console.log(parts[0].name + ":" + parts[1].length); ) .catch(function () console.log("dashboard failed"); ); Try changing Promise.all to Promise.allSettled and log the raw parts to see the shape change. Then point one fetch at /missing and watch which branch runs. Say the combinator name before writing it — naming first is what interviewers listen for. When to use which combinator all for strict coordination, allSettled for best-effort reports, race for timeouts, any for redundant sources. Default to all; anything else should name its reason in a comment. Promise.resolve(2) .then(function (n) n * 10; ) .then(function (n) console.log(n); ); Key takeaways Pending once, then fulfilled or rejected forever; one settlement only. Return from every step or the chain receives undefined. Rejections skip to the nearest catch; unhandled ones crash. References Promise reference. Promise combinators guide. title: Pros and cons, and when not to use JavaScript
description: An honest trade-off list with the real-life cost of each point.
text: Every strength below has a production bill attached. Interviewers ask this to hear judgment, not fandom: pick the tool with your eyes open. Why teams choose it **One language everywhere.** Page, server and tooling share types, utils and hires. Impact: smaller teams ship full features without translators. **Huge ecosystem.** A package exists for nearly everything. Impact: fast starts — plus dependency homework, because anyone can publish. **Event-driven I/O.** Thousands of waiting connections cost little. Impact: chat, feeds and APIs stay responsive on modest hardware. **Instant feedback loop.** Save, refresh, see. Impact: UI iteration speed no compiled stack matches. Why teams regret it **Dynamic typing.** Wrong shapes surface at runtime, not at build. Impact: refactors need tests, and big codebases adopt TypeScript to cope. **Single thread.** One slow loop freezes the page or stalls the server. Impact: CPU work needs chunking, workers or another service. **Fragmented runtimes.** Browsers, Node and edge hosts differ in APIs and versions. Impact: "works here" needs verification matrices and polyfills. **Dependency weight.** Deep install trees inherit other people's bugs and licenses. Impact: audits and lockfiles are non-optional chores. When not to use it Number crunching, games engines and device drivers want compiled languages. Strict real-time control wants deterministic runtimes. And if the team or the target has no JavaScript story (embedded firmware, data science pipelines), forcing one in is resume-driven development. Key takeaways Choose JavaScript for I/O-heavy products and shared page-server code. Budget for types, tests and dependency care from day one. Leave it out of CPU-bound, real-time and non-JS-native domains. References JavaScript language reference. Node learning guides.

title: Interview question bank
description: Every interview question in one searchable list, grouped by topic and level.
text:
Search every question by wording or answer, or filter by topic and level. Your filters live in the URL, so a filtered view can be shared. References JavaScript language reference. Interview questions: What is the difference between var, let and const? `var` is function-scoped and hoisted with the value `undefined`, so it can be
read before its declaration line. `let` and `const` are block-scoped and live
in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs, so reading them early
throws. `const` additionally forbids reassignment, though it does not freeze
objects. Default to `const`, use `let` when the value must change.
 scope hoisting What is hoisting? Hoisting is how declarations are processed before code runs: function
declarations and `var` names are registered during the creation phase, so they
exist from the top of their scope. Only the declaration moves, never the
assignment — `var x = 1` reads as `undefined` before that line. `let` and
`const` are also registered but left uninitialized, which is why touching them
early throws a `ReferenceError` instead.
 hoisting scope What will this log, and why: console.log(x); var x = 5? It logs `undefined`, not an error. The declaration `var x` is hoisted to the
top of the scope, but the assignment `= 5` stays where it is, so at the
`console.log` line `x` exists with the value `undefined`. Change `var` to
`let` and the same code throws, because `let` variables sit in the temporal
dead zone until their declaration line executes.
 hoisting var What is the temporal dead zone? The span of code between entering a block and executing a `let` or `const`
declaration. The name is already registered, so JavaScript knows it exists,
but it is deliberately uninitialized — any read or write throws
`ReferenceError: Cannot access before initialization`. It exists to catch the
classic `var` bug of silently reading `undefined`. The zone ends the moment
the declaration line runs.
 scope let const What is the difference between function scope and block scope? Function scope means a variable is visible everywhere inside the function
that declares it — that is how `var` behaves. Block scope means visibility
ends at the closing brace of the nearest block (`if`, `for`, or a bare
`{ }`) — that is how `let` and `const` behave. A `let` declared inside a
loop body, for example, is a fresh variable per iteration, which is why loop
closures work with `let` and break with `var`.
 scope block Are function declarations hoisted? What about arrow functions in const? Full function declarations are hoisted with their body, so you can call them
before their line in the source. An arrow function stored in `const` is not
callable early: only the `const` name is registered, and it sits in the
temporal dead zone until the assignment runs. Treat declarations as
available-everywhere helpers and `const` arrows as values that must be
defined before use.
 hoisting functions What is shadowing, and is it a problem? Shadowing is declaring a variable with the same name as one in an outer
scope — the inner one wins inside its own scope. It is legal and sometimes
handy (a local `error` hiding an outer one), but it confuses readers and
linters flag it because a small edit can silently change which variable a
line touches. Rename one of them unless the shadowing is clearly deliberate.
 scope Does const make an object immutable? No. `const` only locks the binding — you cannot point the name at a
different object, but you can freely change the object's contents. To freeze
contents you need `Object.freeze`, and even that is shallow: nested objects
stay mutable. For a truly independent copy, clone first (`structuredClone`)
and keep the original `const`.
 const objects What is the difference between == and ===? `===` compares without conversion: different types are never equal.
`==` converts first, using rules nobody fully remembers — `0 == ""` is true,
`null == undefined` is true, `[] == false` is true. Those surprises are the
whole case for `===`: it says exactly what it checks. Use `===` everywhere;
the rare deliberate use of `==` (comparing against `null`) deserves a
comment.
 equality coercion What does typeof return for the main types, including its famous quirk? `typeof` returns `"undefined"`, `"boolean"`, `"number"`, `"bigint"`,
`"string"`, `"symbol"` and `"function"` correctly. The quirk:
`typeof null` is `"object"` — a bug from the first implementation that can
never be fixed without breaking the web. `typeof` also says `"object"` for
arrays, so pair it with `Array.isArray` when arrays matter.
 typeof types What is the difference between null and undefined? `undefined` means no value was ever assigned — a missing argument, a missing
property, a function that returns nothing. `null` means someone deliberately
recorded "nothing here", like an empty cart slot waiting for an item. Rule of
thumb: JavaScript produces `undefined` on its own; `null` in your code should
always be a conscious choice.
 null undefined What is NaN and why does NaN !== NaN? `NaN` is the number value for failed numeric work, like `Number("abc")`. It
is the only value that is not equal to itself, which is why `x !== x` was
once the NaN test. Today use `Number.isNaN(x)`: unlike the global `isNaN`,
it does not coerce first, so `Number.isNaN("abc")` is correctly false. Any
arithmetic touching `NaN` stays `NaN`, which is how one bad parse poisons a
whole total.
 NaN numbers Which values are falsy? Exactly eight: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and
`NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `"0"`, `"false"`, empty arrays
and empty objects, which trip up beginners daily. That is why `if (items)`
cannot detect an empty array; check `items.length` instead. When a value
like `0` or `""` is legitimate input, reach for `??` rather than `||`.
 truthy falsy When does the + operator concatenate and when does it add? `+` adds only when both sides are already numbers (or bigints); if either
side is a string, it converts the other side and concatenates. So
`1 + 2` is `3` but `"1" + 2` is `"12"`, and `"5" - 2` is `3` because `-`
always converts to numbers. A form field total like `price + quantity`
silently becomes `"410"` instead of `5` — convert inputs with `Number()`
first.
 coercion operators What is the difference between || and ?? `||` falls through on any falsy value, so `0 || 10` is `10` — wrong when
zero is a real setting. `??` falls through only on `null` and `undefined`,
so `0 ?? 10` stays `0`. Use `??` for defaults where `0`, `""` or `false`
are valid, and keep `||` for cases where any falsy value should trigger the
fallback.
 operators nullish What is the difference between primitive and reference values? Primitives (strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, `undefined`, symbols,
bigints) are copied by value: changing a copy never touches the original.
Objects, arrays and functions are references: two variables can point at
the same object, and a change through one is visible through the other.
That shared visibility is the source of most state bugs — and the reason
copying objects needs deliberate tools like spread or `structuredClone`.
 types references If two variables point at the same object, what happens when you change one? Both see the change, because neither variable holds the object — each holds
a reference to one shared object in memory. This is why pushing into an
array passed as an argument mutates the caller's array. When you need
independence, create a new object: spread for one level, `structuredClone`
for the whole tree.
 references mutation What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy? A shallow copy duplicates only the top level — nested objects are still
shared references, so editing `copy.address.city` changes the original too.
A deep copy duplicates every level, giving full independence. Spread
(`{...obj}`) and `Array.prototype.slice` are shallow; `structuredClone` is
a deep copy built into the language. Match the tool to how deep the edits
go.
 copying spread What does structuredClone not handle? `structuredClone` copies plain data beautifully but refuses functions (it
throws), drops DOM nodes, and turns class instances into plain objects —
methods and prototypes do not survive. It also cannot clone two objects
that reference each other in some older engines, though modern ones keep
the cycle. For state-shaped data it is the right default; for behavior
(functions, class instances), design the copy by hand.
 structuredClone copying Why does editing a nested object change the original after a spread copy? Spread copies property values, and for a nested object the "value" is a
reference to the same inner object — so the copy and the original share
that inner object. The fix is to spread at every level you edit, or
`structuredClone` the whole thing. A quick tell: if any level below the
top is an object you mutate, one spread is not enough.
 spread mutation How do you compare two objects for equality? `===` on objects only asks "same reference?", so two identical-looking
objects are unequal. For a quick check, compare the fields you care about
directly, or `JSON.stringify` both (fragile: key order and `undefined`
values bite). Libraries offer deep-equal helpers, but in interviews the
expected answer is usually: compare field by field, or avoid needing to by
comparing ids.
 equality objects Why is mutating function arguments considered bad practice? Callers rarely expect their data changed as a side effect — a `sort(cart)`
that reorders the caller's array causes bugs far from the call site and
breaksUI frameworks that detect change by reference. Pure functions that
return new values are predictable and testable. When mutation is the point
(a cache, a builder), name the function so the mutation is obvious.
 mutation functions What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression? A declaration (`function total() {}`) is hoisted whole, so it can run
before its line, and it gets its own `this`. An expression
(`const total = function () {}`) behaves like any other value: it must be
defined before use. In practice declarations suit standalone helpers and
expressions suit callbacks and anything passed around as data.
 functions hoisting How do arrow functions differ from regular functions? Arrows are shorter and inherit `this` from where they are written instead
of getting their own — perfect for callbacks inside methods and array
helpers. The trade is that they cannot be constructors (`new` throws), have
no `arguments` object, and make poor object methods when you need dynamic
`this`. Default to arrows for callbacks; use `function` for methods and
anything constructed.
 arrow this What are default parameters and rest parameters? Defaults fill in missing arguments: `function greet(name = "guest")`
uses `"guest"` when the caller passes `undefined` or nothing. Rest gathers
the leftover arguments into a real array: `function sum(...nums)` lets you
call `sum(1, 2, 3)` and loop `nums` directly. Together they replaced most
`arguments` juggling and manual `undefined` checks.
 parameters rest What is a callback, and what is a higher-order function? A callback is a function handed to another function to run later — a click
handler, a `setTimeout` body, an array mapper. A higher-order function is
the other side: it takes a function in or returns one out, like `map`,
`filter`, or a `once` wrapper. The pair is JavaScript's main reuse
mechanism: behavior travels as values instead of being subclassed.
 callbacks higher-order What is an IIFE and is it still useful? An immediately invoked function expression — `(function () { ... })()` —
runs once and keeps its variables private. Before modules, it was THE scoping
tool: libraries wrapped everything in one to avoid globals. With ES modules
giving every file its own scope, IIFEs are mostly history — you will still
meet them in legacy code and interview trivia, rarely in new code.
 scope IIFE What does the return value of Array.map do, and how is it different from forEach? `map` builds and returns a NEW array with the callback applied to each
item, leaving the original untouched — that return value is the whole
point, so ignoring it is a bug smell. `forEach` returns `undefined` and is
for side effects only (logging, saving, DOM updates). If you are not using
`map`'s result, you wanted `forEach`; if you are pushing inside `forEach`,
you wanted `map`.
 arrays map Explain call, apply and bind. All three set what `this` means inside a function. `call` runs it now with
listed arguments (`fn.call(user, 1, 2)`); `apply` runs it now with an
arguments array (`fn.apply(user, [1, 2])`); `bind` does not run it at all —
it returns a new function with `this` permanently fixed, ideal for handlers
like `button.onclick = save.bind(form)`. Modern code mostly uses `bind` for
callbacks and arrows everywhere else.
 this bind What is a pure function, and why do interviewers care? A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and
touches nothing outside itself — no globals, no mutations, no network. They
are trivial to test, safe to memoize, and painless to parallelize, which is
why functional code and UI frameworks lean on them. The interview angle:
spotting impurity (a hidden mutation, a `Date.now()` inside) is often the
actual bug in the exercise.
 purity testing What is a closure? A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was
created, even after that outer function has finished. The inner function
carries a live link to those variables — not a snapshot — so later calls
see the latest values. Every callback, handler and private counter in
JavaScript leans on this: it is the language's built-in privacy and memory
mechanism.
 closures scope How do closures create private state? Put a variable inside a function and return inner functions that use it:
outsiders can call those functions but never touch the variable directly.
A cart factory returning `add` and `total` keeps `items` hidden — no
property to poke, no global to clash. That is real encapsulation with zero
syntax: the scope boundary IS the privacy boundary.
 closures privacy Why does var in a loop break with setTimeout, and what are the fixes? `var` is function-scoped, so all five iterations share ONE `i`; by the
time the timers run, the loop has finished and every callback logs `5`.
Three fixes: use `let` (fresh binding per iteration), wrap the body in an
IIFE capturing the current value, or pass `i` as an argument. Interviewers
want the mechanism (shared binding vs per-iteration binding), not just the
`let` spell.
 closures var async Do closures capture values or variables? Variables — live links, not snapshots. If the outer variable changes after
the closure is created, the closure sees the new value on its next call.
This surprises people in loops (all callbacks sharing one `var`) and in
effects that read "stale" state. When you need a snapshot, copy the value
into a new variable (or a parameter) at capture time.
 closures scope Where do you meet closures in everyday code? Everywhere a function outlives its creation: event handlers reading outer
settings, `setTimeout` callbacks, `fetch().then()` chains, array mappers
using outer totals, and module-level caches. If you have ever written a
button handler that remembers which item it belongs to, you have shipped a
closure — the interview just wants you to name the mechanism.
 closures callbacks Can closures cause memory leaks? Yes, when a long-lived closure holds a big variable nothing else needs —
a global cache of callbacks, a forgotten timer, an event listener on a
removed element. The garbage collector frees only unreachable memory, and
anything the closure can still reach counts as reachable. Fix: clear the
timer, remove the listener, or null the reference when the feature is done.
 closures memory What is the module pattern, in one sentence each for how and why? How: wrap code in a function (or module) and expose only chosen functions,
keeping the rest in closure scope. Why: it gives private state and a tiny
public surface without any class machinery — the pattern behind countless
libraries before ES modules, and still the mental model for what a module
boundary does.
 closures modules What does a counter function remember between calls? Its closed-over variable. Each call to the outer factory creates a fresh
scope, so two counters from the same factory count independently — that
independence is the giveaway that closures link scopes, not code. If both
counters shared a number, the variable would be outside the factory, and
there would be no closure doing the remembering.
 closures scope Why do React-style effects sometimes see stale values, in closure terms? The effect callback closes over the render's variables — a snapshot of that
moment's props and state. If the effect runs later (a timer, a subscription
callback), it still reads the old render's values, not the current ones.
Fixes all follow the same idea: re-create the closure when values change
(dependencies), read latest values through a ref, or clean up the old
subscription first.
 closures async Explain debounce in terms of closures. Debounce returns a function that closes over a timer id. Each call clears
the pending timer and starts a new one, so the real work runs only after
calls stop for the wait period. The closed-over timer id is the entire
memory of the debouncer — without the closure there would be nowhere
private to keep it. Same story for throttle and `once`.
 closures debounce What decides the value of this in a function? The call site, not the definition site. The same function can see a
different `this` depending on how it is invoked — as a method, as a bare
call, or bound in advance. That single rule explains nearly every `this`
surprise: when context is lost, something changed how the function was
called, usually by passing it as a callback.
 this calls What are the four rules of this? New binding: `new` points `this` at the fresh object. Explicit: `call`,
`apply` or `bind` set it directly. Implicit: calling as `user.save()` sets
it to `user`. Default: a bare call gets `undefined` in strict mode (the
global object in sloppy mode). When rules collide, new beats explicit
beats implicit beats default — memorize that order and most puzzles solve
themselves.
 this rules Why does this become undefined inside a callback like setTimeout? Because passing `user.save` as a callback separates the function from its
object — `setTimeout` later invokes it as a bare function, so the implicit
rule no longer applies and strict mode gives `undefined`. Fixes: wrap it
(`() => user.save()`), which preserves the method-call form, or bind it
once (`user.save.bind(user)`). Losing the dot is losing the receiver.
 this callbacks How do arrow functions treat this? They don't have one. An arrow inherits `this` from the surrounding scope
where it is written, permanently — `call` and `bind` cannot change it.
That makes arrows ideal for callbacks inside methods (the handler keeps the
component) and wrong for object methods or prototype functions that need a
dynamic receiver. If `this` must vary per call, write `function`.
 this arrow What does bind return, and when do you reach for it? `bind` returns a NEW function with `this` (and optionally leading
arguments) locked in; the original is untouched and nothing runs yet.
Reach for it when handing a method to someone else: event listeners,
timers, array callbacks, promises. One `bind` at handoff beats debugging a
mystery `undefined` three stack frames later.
 this bind What is this inside a class, and where does it break? In class methods `this` is the instance — until the method is detached. A
`button.onclick = panel.save` or `setTimeout(panel.save)` call loses the
receiver exactly like plain objects do. The standard fixes are binding in
the constructor, binding at handoff, or defining the handler as an arrow
field (which closes over the instance). Frameworks hit this constantly,
which is why the pattern is worth naming.

title: The this keyword
description: The four rules, arrows, and call, apply and bind.
headings: When to bind, when to arrow
text: this is decided by the call, not the definition — which is why the same method works on its object and breaks the moment you pass it as a callback. Interviewers ask this because "lost context" bugs hide in every event handler and timer. Real-life situation A login form object has a greeting method using this.user. Called as loginForm.greeting(), it works. Handed to a button as a callback, the dot is gone, this is no longer the form, and the greeting shows undefined. Binding once at handoff — or wrapping in an arrow — keeps the receiver. Seen in: React class components bind handlers in the constructor for exactly this reason (React 16, 2017, Component reference). Visual Try it const loginForm = user: "ada", greeting: function () return "hi " + this.user; , ; console.log(loginForm.greeting()); const loose = loginForm.greeting; console.log(loose()); const bound = loginForm.greeting.bind(loginForm); console.log(bound()); function welcome(city) return this.user + " from " + city; console.log(welcome.call(loginForm, "Lagos")); console.log(welcome.apply(loginForm, ["Abuja"])); Try wrapping the callback as function () return loginForm.greeting(); instead of binding. Then try welcome.call(null, "Lagos") and explain it. When to bind, when to arrow Bind (or wrap) at handoff: listeners, timers, array callbacks. Arrow for callbacks written inside methods that must keep the outer this. Never bind an arrow — it has no this to set. const inbox = user: "meera", read: function () return "hi " + this.user; , ; const later = inbox.read; console.log(later()); Key takeaways this comes from the call: method, bare call, explicit set, or new. Losing the dot loses the receiver — bind or wrap at handoff. Arrows inherit this and ignore call, apply and bind. References this reference. bind reference. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Values, references and copying
description: Primitives copy, objects share — plus shallow versus deep copies that hold up.
text: Assigning an object doesn't duplicate it; it hands out another key to the same locker. Interviewers ask this because shared-reference bugs — state edited through an "independent" copy — are the most common UI defects there are. Real-life situation A receipt view aliases the live cart object to format it. Adding a "free gift" line to the receipt silently rewrites the cart total, and the customer is charged for the gift. The fix: format a real copy, so the receipt can never reach back into the cart. Seen in: React state updates replace objects instead of mutating them, so change detection sees a new reference (React 16.8, 2019, useState reference). Visual Try it const cart = items: ["book"], total: 20 ; const receipt = cart; receipt.items.push("pen"); receipt.total = 25; console.log(cart.items.length); console.log(cart.total); const frozen = items: ["book"], total: 20 ; const copy = items: frozen.items.slice(), total: frozen.total ; copy.items.push("pen"); copy.total = 25; console.log(frozen.items.length); console.log(frozen.total); const deep = structuredClone(cart); deep.items.pop(); console.log(cart.items.length); console.log(deep.items.length); Try changing receipt to a spread copy and watch the first two lines. Then change the spread copy to share items and watch them break again. When to copy how Flat data: spread or slice. Nested data you edit: spread every edited level, or structuredClone the whole tree. Data with functions or class instances: copy by hand, because cloners drop behavior. const user = name: "Ada", address: city: "Lagos" ; const copy = ...user ; copy.address.city = "Abuja"; console.log(user.address.city); Key takeaways Primitives copy by value; objects copy by reference. Spread is shallow: nested objects stay shared. structuredClone deep-copies data, but drops functions and prototypes. References Spread syntax. structuredClone. Object equality and references.
