title: Variables, scope and hoisting
description: var versus let and const, the temporal dead zone, and what hoisting really moves.
text: var, let and const all declare variables, but they differ in where the variable is visible and what happens before its line runs. Interviewers ask this because scope bugs — a loop counter leaking, a variable read too early — are silent and everywhere. Real-life situation A checkout page applies a member discount inside an if block. With var, the discount variable leaks out and a later line reuses its stale value for guests. With let and const, each variable stays inside its block and the bug cannot happen. The runner below shows both behaviors side by side. Visual Try it function checkout(price, member) let total = price; if (member) const discount = price * 0.1; total = total - discount; return total; console.log(checkout(100, true)); console.log(checkout(100, false)); console.log(oldWay()); function oldWay() return status; var status = "ready"; try console.log(newWay); catch (error) console.log("tdz: " + error.name); let newWay = "go"; Try changing let total to var total (same result here — why?), then move var status above the return and watch the third line change. When to use which Default to const. Use let when reassignment is the point (counters, accumulators). There is no modern reason to write var — treat it as read-only legacy you will still meet in old codebases. console.log(greet); var greet = "hi"; console.log(greet); Key takeaways var is function-scoped and reads as undefined before its line. let and const are block-scoped and throw before their line (temporal dead zone). Hoisting moves declarations, never assignments. References var statement. let statement. Temporal dead zone. Last verified: 2026-10-12.

title: Why JavaScript was made and where it runs
description: A one-minute timeline from a 10-day prototype to servers, phones and desktops.
text: JavaScript exists because web pages needed to react. In 1995 pages were static documents, and Netscape wanted a small language for buttons, forms and checks that ran instantly in the browser. Interviewers ask this to see whether you know the language's shape — where it belongs and where it doesn't. The story in one timeline **May 1995.** Brendan Eich builds a prototype at Netscape in about 10 days. Its codename is Mocha. **December 1995.** It ships in Netscape Navigator, renamed from LiveScript to JavaScript in a joint announcement with Sun — a marketing nod to Java, a language it never resembled. **1997–2015.** The language is standardized as ECMAScript so every browser implements the same core. The big modernization, ES2015, adds classes, modules, arrows and promises. **2009.** Ryan Dahl releases Node.js, pairing the V8 engine with an event loop so JavaScript runs servers, not just pages. Where it runs today **Browsers and web apps.** Its home: every button, form and feed you touch. **Servers.** Node.js (2009) runs APIs and real-time services in the same language as the page. Seen in: Node.js (nodejs.org, 2009). **Mobile.** Frameworks render native controls from JavaScript. Seen in: React Native (reactnative.dev, 2015). **Desktop apps.** Editors and chat apps ship as web pages in a native shell. Seen in: Visual Studio Code (Wikipedia, 2015), built on Electron. **Serverless.** Platforms run your JavaScript per request with no server to tend — handy for webhooks and scheduled jobs. Last verified: 2026-10-12. Key takeaways JavaScript was a 10-day browser scripting prototype from 1995 that grew up. ECMAScript is the standard; ES2015 is the modern baseline. Node.js took the same language to servers in 2009; phones and desktops followed. References JavaScript language reference. ECMAScript specification. Node.js learning guides.

title: any, unknown, assertions and satisfies
description: Escape hatches, guards, the ! operator and why types are not validation.
text: any disables the checker, unknown forces you to convince it. Interviewers use this pair to separate people who type from people who silence — reach for unknown plus a guard, and say why out loud. Real-life situation Your app parses JSON from an API. The payload could be anything, so unknown is the honest label — then a guard proves it has a string name before you touch it. Typing the same payload any compiles silently and crashes loudly: count + 1 becomes "[object Object]1" with no warning anywhere. Visual Try it function parsePayload(text: string): unknown return JSON.parse(text); const raw = parsePayload(' "name":"sam" '); if (typeof raw === "object" && raw !== null && "name" in raw) const record = raw as name: unknown ; if (typeof record.name === "string") console.log("hello " + record.name); const direct: string = parsePayload('"sam"'); console.log("direct: " + direct); const count: number = raw as number; console.log(count + 1); type LooseTheme = Record ; const theme = color: "blue", size: 12 satisfies LooseTheme; console.log(theme.color + " " + theme.size); console.log(typeof raw); Try changing raw as number to a guarded extraction — the error stays until the types line up, which is the point. Assertions (as) tell the checker what you claim to know; guards (typeof, in, custom is) prove it. satisfies checks a value against a type without widening it. The ! non-null assertion (user!.name) is a promise without proof — the exercise system rejects it, and so should you. Types are never runtime validation: unknown only organizes your own doubt. Real payloads need real checks at the boundary (see typing an API call). const loose: any = name: "sam" ; const name: string = loose.name; console.log(name); Key takeaways unknown plus a guard; any only when you can defend it. Assertions claim, guards prove — prefer proof at boundaries. No annotation validates runtime data; check payloads for real. References TypeScript Handbook: everyday types. TypeScript Handbook: narrowing

title: Basic types and inference
description: Primitives, arrays, tuples, any, unknown, never and as const.
text: You rarely need to annotate everything: TypeScript infers most types and only asks when it cannot know. Interviewers probe whether you can read inference — what type does this variable actually have? Real-life situation A cart total breaks when the string "12" sneaks into a prices array. JavaScript happily computes 0 + "12" as "012" and renders it. With prices: number[], the mistake fails at the line that introduces it, not at the customer. That is the whole pitch for basic types. Visual Try it function cartTotal(prices: number[]): number let total = 0; for (const price of prices) total = total + price; return total; const prices: number[] = [12, 8, 20]; console.log("items: " + prices.length); console.log("total: " + cartTotal(prices)); const pair: [string, number] = ["book", 12]; console.log(pair[0] + " costs " + pair[1]); const frozen = ["book", "pen"] as const; console.log(frozen.length); const typo: number = "12"; console.log("total: " + cartTotal([typo])); Try changing "12" to 12 and watch the error vanish. Then hover over pair and frozen mentally: the tuple keeps position types, while as const freezes the array into readonly literals. Remove the : number[] annotation and nothing changes — inference already knew. Primitives (string, number, boolean) plus null and undefined cover most values. any opts out of checking, unknown forces you to check first, and never marks code that cannot return — each gets its own page later (any versus unknown). const total: number = "five"; console.log(total); Key takeaways Annotate boundaries (function inputs, API shapes); let inference handle the rest. Tuples fix positions, as const freezes literals — arrays do neither. unknown is the honest default for data you have not checked yet. References TypeScript Handbook: everyday types. title: Classes
description: Access modifiers, readonly, parameter properties and implements.
text: Classes bundle state with the operations allowed on it. TypeScript adds compile-time locks — private, protected, readonly — plus a way to promise an interface with implements. Interviewers check you know the locks vanish at runtime. Real-life situation A bank account hides its balance behind deposit and total methods so no caller can set it directly. Marking the owner readonly stops reassignment in the editor — but the emitted JavaScript assigns happily, which the runner below proves. The lock is a promise between developers, not a vault. Visual Try it class BankAccount private balance: number; readonly owner: string; constructor(owner: string, start: number) this.owner = owner; this.balance = start; deposit(amount: number): void this.balance = this.balance + amount; total(): number return this.balance; const mine = new BankAccount("sam", 100); mine.deposit(50); console.log(mine.owner + " has " + mine.total()); mine.owner = "jo"; console.log(mine.total()); Try removing the mine.owner = "jo" line — clean. Then try reading mine.balance from outside: private fails the same way. Parameter properties (constructor(private balance: number)) declare and assign in one stroke, and abstract classes sketch shared behavior subclasses must complete. For this behavior itself, revisit this in the JavaScript topic. class Vault private code = 1234; const vault = new Vault(); console.log(vault.code); Key takeaways private and readonly are editor promises — the emit ignores them. implements checks the class against an interface at declaration time. Parameter properties and abstract remove whole lines of boilerplate. References TypeScript Handbook: classes. MDN: classes.

title: Will it compile puzzles
description: Twelve type puzzles with real compiler diagnostics.
text: Twelve puzzles, same rules as interviews: read, commit to Yes or No (and the failing line), then reveal the real diagnostics. Every reveal shows what the pinned compiler actually reported — the machine grades you, not your confidence. interface Account id: number; name: string; const account: Account = id: 1, name: "sam", nickname: "s" ; console.log(account); function shout(text: string | null): string if (text === null) return ""; return text.toUpperCase(); console.log(shout("hi")); const scores: readonly number[] = [10, 20]; scores.push(30); console.log(scores); const mixed: string | number = "a"; const exact: number = mixed; console.log(exact); function identity (value: T): T return value; const word: string = identity("hello"); console.log(word); interface Scores [player: string]: number; const table: Scores = sam: 3, jo: "many" ; console.log(table); const payload: any = count: "three" ; const count: number = payload.count; console.log(count); function fail(message: string): never throw new Error(message); const name: string = fail("boom"); console.log(name); function greet(name?: string): string return name; console.log(greet()); const raw: unknown = "preview"; const text: string = raw as string; console.log(text); const pair: [string, number] = ["a", 1]; pair.push(2); console.log(pair); const names: string[] = ["sam", "jo"]; const first: string = names[0]; console.log(first); References TypeScript Handbook: narrowing. title: Enums, const assertions and literal unions
description: When an enum earns its keep, and when a union of strings wins.
text: "New, paid, shipped, done" — a fixed set of names. TypeScript offers two ways to model it, and interviewers want the trade-off, not just the syntax. Real-life situation An order tracker stores its status in a database column and renders it in a dropdown. A string union ("new" | "paid" | ...) erases completely and matches the stored text exactly. A numeric enum emits a real lookup object — handy when you need reverse mapping, but a second source of truth to keep in sync with the database. Visual Try it type OrderStatus = "new" | "paid" | "shipped" | "done"; function next(status: OrderStatus): OrderStatus if (status === "new") return "paid"; if (status === "paid") return "shipped"; return "done"; enum OldStatus New = 0, Paid = 1, Shipped = 2, console.log(next("new")); console.log(next("paid")); console.log(OldStatus.Paid); console.log(next("refunded")); Try changing "refunded" to "shipped" — clean, printing "done". Notice OldStatus.Paid prints 1: numeric enums exist at runtime, while the union vanished entirely. as const objects give a middle path — real values plus literal types — without enum quirks. Default stance: reach for the string union. Take the enum when you need runtime values (numeric codes, reverse lookups) and accept the emitted object. const enum avoids the object but complicates isolated builds — say that sentence in interviews and move on. enum Direction Up = 0, Down = 1, const d: Direction = Direction.Up; console.log(d); Key takeaways String unions erase fully and match stored text — the default choice. Numeric enums emit a runtime object; that is the whole cost. as const gives values plus literal types without enum machinery. References TypeScript Handbook: enums. TypeScript Handbook: everyday types.

title: Functions
description: Parameters, returns, optional and default values, and callbacks.
text: Function signatures are contracts callers cannot wiggle out of: how many arguments, in what order, of which types, and what comes back. Interviewers test whether you read a signature the way the compiler does — positionally, not by name. Real-life situation A payment helper takes an amount and a currency. Someone calls it as chargeCard("USD", 25) — names swapped. JavaScript charges twenty-five "USD"s at runtime; TypeScript rejects the call before review. Add an optional tip with a default, and the signature documents itself better than any comment. Visual Try it function chargeCard(amount: number, currency: string): string const label = amount + " " + currency; return "charged " + label; function withTip(amount: number, tip: number = 0): number return amount + tip; function runTwice(task: () => void): void task(); task(); console.log(chargeCard(25, "USD")); console.log(withTip(20)); console.log(withTip(20, 5)); runTwice(function () console.log("receipt printed"); ); console.log(chargeCard("USD", 25)); Try fixing the last line to chargeCard(25, "USD") — the Types tab goes clean. Then change runTwice's parameter to (code: number) => void and watch the anonymous function fail: callbacks are checked against the parameter they are passed to, which is why inline handlers usually need no annotations at all. Optional parameters (tip?: number) may be skipped; default parameters (tip = 0) fill themselves in. Overloads — several signatures, one implementation — appear in library definitions; you will read them far more often than you write them. For function values, see also closures in the JavaScript topic. function total(price: number, tax: number): number return price + tax; const bill: number = total(10, "5"); console.log(bill); Key takeaways Arguments match positionally: order and count are part of the contract. Defaults document themselves; callbacks inherit types from context. void means "ignore the result", not "returns nothing usable". References TypeScript Handbook:

title: Generics
description: Reusable functions and interfaces with constraints and defaults.
text: Generics let one definition serve many types without surrendering checking. Interviewers ask for the one-line version first — "a placeholder the caller fills in" — then probe constraints and defaults. Real-life situation Every API response in your app has the same envelope (data plus status) but different payloads. Without generics you duplicate the interface per endpoint or fall back to any. With ApiResponse , each call fills in its own T and keeps full checking — one definition, every endpoint typed. Visual Try it interface ApiResponse data: T; status: number; function wrap (value: T): ApiResponse return data: value, status: 200 ; function first (items: T[]): T | undefined return items[0]; const names = wrap(["a", "b"]); console.log(names.status); console.log(first(names.data)); const n: number = wrap(5).data; console.log(n + 1); const broken: string = wrap(5).data; console.log(broken); Try fixing the last two lines to const broken: number = ... — clean. Notice wrap(["a", "b"]) needed no explicit type argument: inference fills T from the call. Constraints (T extends id: number ) demand a minimum shape, and defaults (T = string) kick in when the caller says nothing. Generics also carry interfaces (Box ), classes, and type aliases. The rule of thumb: generic over what varies per call, concrete about everything else. function wrap (value: T): T[] return [value]; const xs: number[] = wrap(1); console.log(xs); Key takeaways T is filled per call — by inference first, explicitly when needed. Constrain with extends to demand a shape; default with =. One generic definition beats N copies or a silent any. References TypeScript Handbook: generics. TypeScript Handbook: everyday types.

title: How TypeScript works
description: Compile time versus runtime, checking versus emit, and how people run it.
text: TypeScript does its work before your code ever runs, then gets out of the way. Two distinctions carry every interview answer: checking is not emit, and compile time is not runtime. Visual Compile time versus runtime Checking asks "could this be wrong?" Emit asks "what JavaScript should ship?" They are independent: even with errors, the compiler still emits (try it below — the runner tells you plainly when it does). At runtime no type information remains, so no instanceof trick can recover an interface. If you need safety from real data, you validate at runtime; types only describe what you claimed. Structural typing fits here too: two types with the same shape are compatible, whatever their names. The snippet below passes because coords has everything Point asks for — no declaration of intent. How people run TypeScript Most projects compile with tsc or let a bundler strip types during the build. For running directly: Node.js executes TypeScript files itself since v22.6.0, enabled by default since v22.18.0 and v23.6.0, and stable since v24.12.0 — but it only strips types, never checks them (Node.js TypeScript docs). Community runners like tsx go further with full transformation. And since July 2026, the tsc binary in the typescript package is the native Go compiler; programmatic users stay on the 6.x line (see the 7.0 announcement). Try it function cartTotal(prices: number[]): number let total = 0; for (const price of prices) total = total + price; return total; console.log("total: " + cartTotal([12, 8, 20])); const typo: number = "12"; console.log("total: " + cartTotal([typo])); Run it, then read both tabs: the Types tab reports the mismatch while the Output tab still prints. Change "12" to 12 and watch the Types tab go quiet. That split — noisy at compile time, silent at runtime — is the mental model behind every page that follows. References TypeScript Handbook: everyday types. Node.js TypeScript docs. Announcing TypeScript 7.0. Last verified: 2026-10-13.

title: Migrating a JavaScript project
description: AllowJs, checkJs, JSDoc and a five-step path that never stalls.
text: Nobody rewrites a working app in a weekend. Migration is a ratchet: check the JavaScript you have, annotate the seams, rename files one by one, and tighten strictness last. Interviewers ask for the order — recite these five steps. Real-life situation A checkout helper has grown for two years with no types. Step one flips on checkJs so the compiler reads the existing JavaScript. Step two adds JSDoc annotations to the trickiest function. Steps three and four rename one file to .ts and fix only its errors. Step five raises strictness. Each step ships; the build never goes red for a week. Visual Try it async function loadUserIds(): Promise try const response = await fakeFetch("https://api.example.com/users"); const users = (await response.json()) as Array ; return users.map(function (user) return user.id; ); catch (e) console.log("failed: " + e.message); return []; loadUserIds().then(function (ids) console.log("ids: " + ids.join(",")); ); Try narrowing the catch variable — e instanceof Error ? e.message : "unknown" — and the Types tab goes clean. That is step four in miniature: one file, one error species, fixed and shipped. allowJs lets .js files stay in the build during the transition, checkJs types them loosely, and JSDoc (@param number[] prices) annotates without renaming anything. let nickname: string; console.log(nickname); nickname = "sam"; Key takeaways Check first (checkJs), annotate second (JSDoc), rename third, strict last. Fix one error species at a time; every step must ship green. allowJs keeps old files building while new files get full checking. References TypeScript Handbook: migrating from JavaScript. TypeScript Handbook: JSDoc reference.

title: Modules and declaration files
description: import type, .d.ts bridges, @types and the declare keyword.
text: Your typed code constantly meets untyped JavaScript: libraries, legacy files, globals. Declaration files (.d.ts) describe those neighbors so the checker can verify your side of the conversation. Interviewers ask "where do the types for lodash come from?" — this page is that answer. Real-life situation You install a small slug helper written in plain JavaScript. No annotations, no checking — every call is a guess. A declaration file bridges the gap: it promises slugify(text: string): string without touching the library, and suddenly wrong calls fail in your editor. When a library ships no types, the community DefinitelyTyped collection (@types/... packages) usually has them. Visual Try it function slugify(text: string): string return text.trim().toLowerCase().split(" ").join("-"); const shopVersion = "2.1.0"; type Slugify = typeof slugify; function productSlug(name: string, make: Slugify): string const clean = name.trim().toLowerCase(); return make(clean); function versionLabel(prefix: string, version: string): string return prefix + " v" + version; const make: Slugify = slugify; console.log(productSlug(" Red Chair ", make)); console.log(versionLabel("shop", shopVersion)); console.log(make("Tea Pot")); const code: number = shopVersion; console.log("code " + code); Try changing the code annotation to string — clean. typeof borrows a value's type without repeating it, which is exactly what a .d.ts file contains: declare function slugify(text: string): string; — a promise with no body. import type brings in only the type meaning, so bundlers can drop the import entirely (Node's own type stripping needs that keyword to erase imports correctly). The static version of the bridge, build-checked below, shows the typed side: the same promises a .d.ts file would hold, with bodies so the page can verify them. The real .d.ts would contain only the declare lines (shown as inline code above, never executed). For JavaScript-side module mechanics, see modules in the JavaScript topic

title: Objects: interface versus type
description: Optional and readonly fields, index signatures, and the classic question.
text: Objects are where TypeScript earns its keep: one shape declaration protects every function that touches an API user. Interviewers ask "interface versus type?" on almost every loop — the answer is short, and below. Real-life situation An API returns users with optional emails and occasional extra fields. Without a declared shape, every consumer re-guesses: is email always there? With interface ApiUser, the optionality lives in one place, and a misspelled extra property fails immediately instead of silently passing undefined downstream. Visual Try it interface ApiUser id: number; name: string; email?: string; function label(user: ApiUser): string const suffix = user.email === undefined ? "" : " "; return user.name + suffix; const reader: ApiUser = id: 1, name: "sam" ; console.log(label(reader)); console.log(label( id: 2, name: "jo", email: "jo@x.com" )); type Admin = ApiUser & level: number ; const boss: Admin = id: 3, name: "al", level: 2 ; console.log(label(boss) + " level " + boss.level); const levels: Record = al: 2 ; console.log(levels.al); console.log(label( id: 4, name: "zo", nickname: "z" )); Try removing nickname from the last call — clean. Then add readonly before id and attempt reassignment: the compiler stops you, although JavaScript itself would allow it. That gap (compile-time promise, no runtime lock) surprises people once, then never again. So interface or type? Interfaces describe object shapes and merge across declarations; type aliases cover everything else (unions, tuples, mapped shapes) and combine with &. For plain objects they are interchangeable — say that, then mention extending versus intersection. interface Card id: number; name: string; const card: Card = id: 1, name: "x", nickname: "y" ; console.log(card); Key takeaways Declare the shape once; every consumer inherits the optionality rules. Excess property checks only bite fresh literals — that is the feature. interface for object shapes, type for everything composed. References TypeScript

title: Pros and cons
description: Honest trade-offs of TypeScript, and when not to use it.
text: TypeScript pays for itself on teams and long-lived code, and charges rent everywhere else. Interviewers ask "when wouldn't you use it?" to check you see both sides — memorize the honest version below. Where it wins Refactors stop being scary: rename a field and the compiler lists every caller you missed. Onboarding gets faster because signatures document themselves — a new hire reads chargeCard(amount: number, currency: string) instead of guessing. Typos and swapped arguments fail in the editor, minutes after writing, instead of in production weeks later. Where it costs Small scripts and prototypes move slower: every quick experiment wants annotations, config, and a build step. Library boundaries leak complexity — someone must write and maintain type definitions, and advanced types can puzzle readers more than the runtime code they describe. Build times grow with project size (one reason the native 7.0 compiler landed in 2026), and types can never validate external data: an API can still send whatever it wants at runtime. When not to use it Skip it for throwaway scripts, one-off migrations, and tiny static pages with no logic worth checking. Skip the strictest settings on week one of a brownfield migration — partial adoption beats an all-or-nothing stall (see migrating a JavaScript project). And never treat a green check as proof: it proves consistency with your annotations, not with reality. References TypeScript Handbook: introduction. Announcing TypeScript 7.0.

title: Interview question bank
description: Every TypeScript interview question in one searchable list.
text:
Search every question by wording or answer, or filter by topic and level. Your filters live in the URL, so a filtered view can be shared. References TypeScript Handbook. Interview questions: What is TypeScript? TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript maintained alongside the
`typescript` compiler package. You write `.ts` files with optional type
annotations, then the compiler checks them and emits plain `.js` you can
run anywhere JavaScript runs. Valid JavaScript is usually valid TypeScript,
so you can adopt it gradually. Think of it as JavaScript plus a static
checker that catches mistakes before your code runs.
 basics intro Why would you choose TypeScript over plain JavaScript? You get earlier feedback on the mistakes JavaScript hides until runtime:
misspelled properties, wrong argument shapes, and forgotten `null` cases.
Types also act as living documentation, so you spend less time guessing what
a function expects. Editors use them for precise autocomplete and safe
renames. For teams and long-lived codebases, that means fewer runtime
surprises and faster refactors, at the cost of writing and maintaining
the annotations.
 benefits teams What changed with TypeScript 7's native compiler? TypeScript 7, released July 8 2026, ships a native compiler written in Go
inside the `typescript` package for much faster checking and builds. The
native compiler does not offer a programmatic JavaScript API, so tools that
called the old API should use the `@typescript/typescript6` compatibility
package, which provides the `tsc6` binary and re-exports the 6.0 API.
Everyday `tsc` command-line usage stays familiar.
 toolchain compiler What kinds of bugs does TypeScript catch for you? It catches shape mismatches: calling a function with the wrong arguments,
reading a property that does not exist, or assuming a value is defined when
it can be `null`. It also flags misspelled names and incorrect assignments
across files, which plain JavaScript would only reveal at runtime. You still
need tests for logic errors, but the compiler removes a whole class of
silly wiring mistakes before you even run the code.
 bugs safety When does TypeScript check your types? It checks statically, before your code runs — when your editor highlights
an error or when you run `tsc` in your build. Nothing about the check
survives into the emitted JavaScript. That means a passing check tells you
the code was consistent at build time, not that runtime data will match.
Data from an API or user input still needs runtime validation, because the
compiler cannot see what the network will send.
 checking build How does the tsc compiler turn TypeScript into JavaScript? You run `tsc` over your `.ts` files and it does two jobs: it checks your
types against each other, then it strips the type syntax and emits plain
`.js`. Modern syntax is downleveled to match your `target`, so optional
chaining or classes still run on older runtimes. You configure the input,
output folder, and language level in `tsconfig.json`, and the emitted files
are what you actually deploy and run.
 tsc compile What does it mean that TypeScript types are erasable? It means every annotation, interface, and type alias is removed when the
code is emitted — no trace remains at runtime. The emitted JavaScript
behaves exactly as if you had written it by hand without types. You cannot
inspect an interface in running code or branch on it, because it no longer
exists. If you need a runtime check, you must write real JavaScript logic
such as a `typeof` test or a validation function.
 erasable emit Does TypeScript do any runtime type checking? No, the compiler performs no runtime checking itself. Once your `.ts` is
emitted to `.js`, all types are gone and execution follows normal JavaScript
rules — a wrong-typed API response flows straight through. The safety comes
entirely from the build-time check plus the runtime guards you write
yourself. That is why teams pair TypeScript with small validators at
program boundaries, where outside data enters typed code.
 runtime checking How can Node.js run .ts files directly with type stripping? Recent Node versions can run `.ts` files by stripping the type syntax
without doing any type checking, so development feels instant. The feature
first appeared around v22.6.0, became enabled by default through the v22
and v23 line, and stabilized later — check your exact Node version before
relying on it. Remember it only removes types: type errors still run, and
syntax Node cannot strip cleanly needs a real build step.
 node stripping If tsc reports a type error, does it still emit JavaScript? By default yes — checking and emitting are separate steps, so `tsc` prints
the errors but still writes `.js` output unless you set `noEmitOnError`.
That surprises beginners who expect errors to block the build. In practice
you decide: leave the default for quick iteration, or enable
`noEmitOnError` in CI so broken types cannot ship. Either way, fix the
reported errors — the emitted code still runs as plain JavaScript.
 tsc emit What tools besides tsc can compile TypeScript? Many tools transpile TypeScript by stripping types without full checking:
`esbuild`, `swc`, `tsx`, and bundlers built on them compile single files
very fast. That speed is ideal for development and bundling, but none of
them replaces `tsc` for correctness — they happily emit code with type
errors. A common setup uses a fast transpiler to build and runs `tsc
--noEmit` alongside it purely to check types.
 tooling transpile What are the main benefits of TypeScript? You catch wiring mistakes early, document intent in the code itself, and get
far better editor help — accurate jumps, autocomplete, and renames that
update every caller. Refactors that feel risky in JavaScript become
mechanical: change a shape and the compiler lists every place to fix. For
shared libraries, published `.d.ts` files let consumers use your API
correctly without reading the source. The payoff grows with codebase size
and team size.
 benefits refactor What are the main costs of adopting TypeScript? You pay in setup and upkeep: a build step, a `tsconfig.json` to maintain,
and annotations to write for every boundary. Third-party libraries
occasionally need extra `@types` packages or small local declarations.
Beginners also fight the compiler at first, especially around `null` and
third-party shapes. For tiny scripts the overhead can outweigh the help,
so weigh the long-term maintenance win against the short-term slowdown.
 costs tradeoffs When should you NOT use TypeScript? Skip it for throwaway scripts, quick prototypes, and tiny automations where
a build step slows you down more than types help. It also adds friction to
highly dynamic code — heavy metaprogramming or loosely shaped plugin
systems can force you into `any` everywhere, defeating the purpose. If your
team will not maintain the types, an untyped codebase with good tests beats
a half-typed one that everyone ignores. Choose the tool that fits the
lifespan of the code.
 tradeoffs judgment How does TypeScript compare to JavaScript with JSDoc type checking? Both give you editor help and `tsc` checking, but JSDoc keeps you in plain
`.js` with types written as comments, while TypeScript uses dedicated `.ts`
syntax. JSDoc suits gradual adoption or teams that cannot add a build step,
since the code runs as-is. Full TypeScript scales better: its syntax stays
readable for complex generics, and refactoring tools understand it more
reliably. You can even mix them with `allowJs` and `checkJs` during a
migration.
 jsdoc migration What are the most common basic types in TypeScript? You will use `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, and `undefined` for
everyday values, plus `bigint` and `symbol` for rarer cases. Arrays are
written `string[]` and objects get inline shapes like `{ name: string }`.
`void` marks functions that return nothing useful. Start with these small
building blocks — every interface, union, and generic you meet later is
composed from them.
 basics annotations How do you add a type annotation to a variable? You add a colon plus the type after the name, like `let name: string =
'Asha'`. The annotation tells the compiler what you intend, and it rejects
any later assignment that disagrees. You only need it where inference cannot
figure things out — for empty declarations like `let user: User` or
function boundaries. Inside a function body, prefer letting inference do
the work so the code stays quiet.
 syntax annotations How does type inference work, and when should you rely on it? The compiler infers a type from the initializer, so `let count = 0` is
treated as `number` without you writing anything. Rely on it for locals —
it keeps code short and stays accurate. Write explicit annotations at
function parameters and return positions, where there is no initializer to
learn from and where the annotation documents your contract for every
caller. Hover over a variable in your editor to see what was inferred.
 inference basics How do null and undefined differ in TypeScript? `undefined` means a value is missing — an uninitialized variable or a
skipped optional property. `null` means you deliberately set emptiness, like
clearing a selected user. With `strictNullChecks` on, they are distinct
types and you must handle each before use, which removes the classic
`Cannot read properties of null` crash. Be explicit about which one your
function accepts and returns.
 null undefined How do you type arrays in TypeScript? You write the element type plus brackets, like `string[]` or `number[]`,
which is shorthand for `Array<string>`. The compiler then checks every
element on creation and every access afterwards — pushing a `number` into a
`string[]` is an error. Use `readonly string[]` when callers should not
mutate the array. For fixed-length mixed shapes, reach for a tuple instead
of a plain array.
 arrays basics What is a tuple and when would you use one? A tuple is a fixed-length array where each position has its own type, like
`[string, number]` for a name-age pair. You annotate it with brackets
around the sequence, and the compiler checks both the length and each
slot's type. Use tuples for small, positionally meaningful returns such as
`[user, error]` helpers. For anything with named fields, prefer an object —
names document intent better than positions do.
 tuples arrays What does void mean as a function return type? `void` means the function returns nothing you should use — typical for
callbacks, event handlers, and side-effect helpers. You can still `return`
early with no value, but assigning the result is pointless. Do not confuse
it with `undefined` as a value type: `void` describes intent at the
function boundary, while `undefined` is a concrete value that can appear
anywhere. Annotate effect-only functions `: void` to keep callers honest.
 void functions What does never mean, and when do you see it? `never` marks values that cannot occur: a function that always throws or
loops forever, or a code branch that should be unreachable. You meet it most
in exhaustive `switch` statements, where narrowing every union member leaves
`never` in the final `default` — assigning anything there proves a case was
missed. It also appears when you intersect incompatible types. Treat a
`never` sighting as the compiler telling you this path is impossible.
 never narrowing How do you describe the shape of an object in TypeScript? You write an object literal type naming each property and its type, like
`{ name: string; age: number }`. The compiler then requires those exact
properties with compatible values. Add `?` for optional members and
`readonly` for fields that must not be reassigned. For reused shapes, lift
the literal into an `interface` or `type` alias so every function shares
one named contract instead of repeating the literal.
 objects shapes What is the difference between interface and type? Both name an object shape, and for everyday use they are interchangeable.
An `interface` can be extended with `extends` and re-opened across
declarations, which libraries use to augment shapes. A `type` alias can
additionally name unions, tuples, and mapped shapes that an interface
cannot express. As a rule of thumb, use `interface` for public object
contracts and `type` when you need unions or computed transformations.
 interface type How do optional properties work? You add `?` after the name, like `nickname?: string`, which lets callers
omit the property entirely. Inside your code the value reads as `string |
undefined`, so you must handle the missing case before using it. Keep
optional fields for genuinely absent data, not for values you always set —
overusing `?` pushes `undefined` checks onto every reader. Pair optionals
with defaults or narrowing at the point of use.
 optional objects What does readonly do on a property? It forbids reassignment after creation, so `readonly id: string` can be set
once in the object literal or constructor and never changed again. The
compiler rejects later writes, which protects identifiers and shared
config. Note it is a compile-time guard only — the emitted JavaScript still
allows the write at runtime. For arrays, use `readonly T[]` or
`Readonly<T>` to get the same one-way protection across the whole shape.
 readonly safety What are excess property checks? When you pass a fresh object literal to a typed position, the compiler
rejects unknown extra properties — passing `{ name, age, nick }` where only
`{ name, age }` is expected is an error. It catches your typos instead of
silently ignoring the extra field. The check only applies to fresh
literals; assigning through a variable skips it. If extras are legitimate,
add an index signature or extend the target type rather than working
around the error.
 excess literals How do you extend an interface or combine object types? You extend an interface with `extends`, like `interface Admin extends User
{ level: number }`, which inherits every member of `User` plus the new
ones. With type aliases you intersect instead: `type Admin = User & {
level: number }`. Both produce one flattened shape the compiler checks as
a whole. Prefer `extends` for clear hierarchies and intersections when you
compose small reusable pieces. Conflicting property types in an
intersection become `never`.
 extends intersection What is structural typing? TypeScript checks what an object contains, not what class or interface name
it was declared with. If a function wants `{ name: string }`, any object
with at least a string `name` is accepted — extra properties are fine and no
explicit `implements` is needed. That keeps plain object literals and
third-party shapes interoperable. The tradeoff is that two unrelated shapes
with the same members look identical to the checker, so use branding or
literal tags when identity matters.
 structural shapes How do index signatures work? They describe objects with unknown keys but known value types, like `{ [key:
string]: number }` for a score table. You read and write any string key and
the compiler enforces the value type. Use them for dictionaries and lookup
maps, but prefer explicit properties or `Record` unions when the keys are
known — named fields document intent and catch typos that an open index
signature would silently accept.
 index record How do you type a function's parameters and return value? You annotate each parameter and the result, like `function add(a: number, b:
number): number`. Parameters need explicit types because there is nothing
to infer them from, while the return annotation documents the contract for
callers. The compiler then rejects wrong-typed arguments and checks that
every code path returns a compatible value. Keep the annotations at the
boundary and let locals inside the body infer.
 functions annotations How do optional and default parameters work? You mark a trailing parameter `name?: string` to let callers skip it, or
give it a default like `name = 'guest'` which makes it optional
automatically. Optional parameters read as possibly `undefined` inside the
body, so handle that case. Keep required parameters first — a required
parameter after an optional one confuses callers and needs an explicit
`undefined` argument. Defaults also document the common case right in the
signature.
 optional defaults How do you type an arrow function or callback? You annotate it inline like `(user: User) => user.name`, and the return
type is usually inferred. When passing a callback directly, you can often
omit annotations entirely — the expected function type provides context, so
`(u) => u.name` is checked against the parameter's declared signature. This
contextual typing keeps event handlers and array callbacks quiet. Add
explicit annotations only when the callback stands alone without context.
 arrow callbacks How do function overloads work? You write several call signatures above one implementation, each describing
a supported way to call the function. Callers see only the overload list,
while the implementation signature stays hidden and must accept them all.
Use overloads when one function genuinely accepts different shapes, like
`pad(s: string)` versus `pad(n: number)`. If the variants can be expressed
as one union or optional-parameter signature, prefer that — it is shorter
and easier to maintain.
 overloads signatures How do you type a function that takes no useful result, like a click handler? You annotate the return as `void`, like `(e: MouseEvent) => void`, to show
the result is ignored. Handlers, loggers, and `forEach` callbacks all use
this shape. Callers can pass functions that happen to return something —
TypeScript allows that — but nobody should read the value. Reserve `never`
for functions that never return at all, such as ones that always throw.
 void handlers How do rest parameters work with types? You collect trailing arguments with `...rest: string[]`, which reads inside
the body as a normal array. Callers can pass any number of extra arguments
and each is checked against the element type. Tuples make rest precise: `...
args: [string, number?]` enforces the exact sequence. Use rest for
wrappers like loggers and forwarders where the arity varies, and prefer
fixed parameters when the count is known.
 rest tuples How do you type an async function? You annotate the unwrapped value inside `Promise`, like `async function
load(): Promise<User>`. The `async` keyword wraps your `return` and `throw`
into the promise for you, so you write the body as if it were synchronous.
Callers must `await` or `.then` the result. For error paths, let the
promise reject with an `Error` rather than resolving a union — it keeps
`try/catch` at the call site natural.
 async promise How do you write a reusable function type? You alias the signature, like `type Handler = (id: string) => void`, then
reuse `Handler` for every matching function. It keeps callbacks consistent
across components and makes refactors one-line changes. For methods inside
objects, you can write the shorthand `{ onSave(id: string): void }`. Name
the alias after its role, not its shape, so readers learn intent from the
name alone.
 aliases callbacks What is a union type? A value that can be one of several types, written with `|` like `string |
number`. You use it when a variable, parameter, or response genuinely holds
different shapes at different times. The compiler forces you to handle each
member before using type-specific features — you cannot call string methods
until you have narrowed away the `number` case. Keep unions small and
meaningful so every branch is worth handling.
 unions basics How do you narrow a union with typeof? You guard with `typeof value === 'string'` inside an `if`, and the compiler
shrinks the union to that branch — `string` in the true path, the remainder
in the `else`. It works for primitives like `string`, `number`, and
`boolean`. Write the check as a plain condition so it also guards at
runtime. For objects, switch to `in`, `instanceof`, or a literal tag check
instead.
 narrowing typeof What is a discriminated union? A union of object types that share one literal tag field, like `{ k

title: TypeScript in a React app and an API call
description: Typing props, state, events, a fetch hook and an API response.
text: Components are functions with typed inputs; API calls are promises with typed outputs. Interviewers ask you to type both live — props with an interface, fetch with a generic envelope, and state that cannot hold the wrong shape. Real-life situation A login form takes a title and an onLogin callback, fetches the user, and renders the name. Untyped, the callback receives whatever the form feels like and the render trusts whatever the network sent. Typed, props are checked at every usage, the response envelope is generic, and a runtime guard stands where the network ends and your code begins. Visual Try it interface ApiUser id: number; name: string; email: string; interface ApiResponse data: T; status: number; async function loadUser(id: number): Promise > const response = await fakeFetch("https://api.example.com/users/" + id); const data = (await response.json()) as ApiUser; return data: data, status: response.status ; function isUser(value: unknown): value is ApiUser return ( typeof value === "object" && value !== null && "name" in value && "email" in value ); loadUser(1).then(function (res: ApiResponse ) console.log(res.status + " " + res.data.name); console.log(isUser(res.data) ? "valid" : "invalid"); const bad: ApiUser = res.data.name; console.log(bad); ); Try fixing bad to res.data — clean. Props typing follows the same shape-first habit, shown statically below with small declared helpers standing in for React (no imports in the sandbox): The event parameter needed no annotation — context provides it. State keeps the type of its initial value. And the guard (isUser) is the honest part: types describe your claims, but only a runtime check confronts the network. interface CardProps title: string; count: number; function renderCard(props: CardProps): string return props.title + props.count; renderCard( count: 3 ); Key takeaways Props are interfaces; events and state inherit types from context. Wrap fetch in a generic envelope, then guard the payload at runtime. A gre

title: tsconfig and strict mode
description: What strict turns on, what each flag catches, and target versus lib.
text: tsconfig.json is where a project sets its standards: how strict the checker is, what language level to emit, and which built-in libraries exist. Interviewers ask "what does strict actually enable?" — strict: true is one switch arming a family of flags. Real-life situation A legacy project turns strict on and fifty errors appear overnight. Almost all are real: an undefined passed as a name, a variable read before assignment, a null nobody admitted. Each flag below catches one species — strictNullChecks (no silent undefined), noImplicitAny (no silent any), strictPropertyInitialization and friends. Turning them on file by file beats turning them off forever. Visual Try it function initials(first: string, last: string): string return first[0] + last[0]; const pair = ["sam", "jo"]; console.log(initials(pair[0], pair[1])); function greet(user: name: string ): string return "hi " + user.name; console.log(greet( name: "sam" )); function pickName(known: boolean): string | undefined return known ? "jo" : undefined; const maybe = pickName(true); console.log(greet( name: maybe )); function firstTag(tags: string[]): string const found = tags.find(function (t) return t.length > 0; ); return (found ?? "none").toUpperCase(); console.log(firstTag(["a", "bb"])); console.log(firstTag([])); Try changing pickName's return type to string — the Types tab goes quiet, because the checker trusts the new promise. target chooses the emitted language level (this topic uses ES2022) while lib chooses which built-ins exist (DOM for browsers). Our sandbox pins both, and every runner labels its mode. With strict off, the same code compiles silently — the override below is displayed, exactly as the page promises: const maybe: string | undefined = ["sam", "jo"][2]; function greet(user: name: string ): string return "hi " + user.name; console.log(greet( name: maybe )); const name: string = undefined; console.log(name); Key takeaways strict: true arms the flag family — null checks and no silent any firs

title: Unions, literals and narrowing
description: typeof, in and discriminated unions that shrink types line by line.
text: Unions say "one of these"; narrowing proves "this one, here". Interviewers love this page because it is TypeScript thinking in pure form: start wide, test, and watch the type shrink inside each branch. Real-life situation A fetch can be loading, successful, or failed — three shapes, one variable. Without a union you juggle flags and nullable fields; with a discriminated union on status, each branch knows exactly which fields exist. Accessing users inside the "success" branch is safe because the check already proved the shape. Visual Try it type FetchState = | status: "loading" | status: "success"; users: string[] | status: "error"; message: string ; function describe(state: FetchState): string if (state.status === "loading") return "still loading"; if (state.status === "success") return state.users.length + " users"; return "failed: " + state.message; console.log(describe( status: "loading" )); console.log(describe( status: "success", users: ["a", "b"] )); console.log(describe( status: "error", message: "down" )); console.log(describe( status: "done" )); Try changing "done" to "error" with a message — clean. The guards that shrink types are small: typeof for primitives, in for object shapes, instanceof for class instances, and equality on a shared literal field for discriminated unions. A custom type guard (value is User) teaches the checker a test you wrote yourself. The compiler verifies each narrowed type below at build time: const direction: "up" | "down" = "left"; console.log(direction); Key takeaways Model "one of" with unions; prove "this one" with a guard per branch. Discriminated unions (one shared literal field) scale best. Narrowing is compile-time only — the emitted JavaScript keeps the tests. References TypeScript Handbook: narrowing. TypeScript Handbook: everyday types.

title: Utility types, keyof and typeof
description: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record and the queries that power them.
text: Utility types derive new shapes from old ones, so one source interface feeds forms, previews, and API payloads without drift. Interviewers ask you to build Partial from scratch — the pattern matters more than the name. Real-life situation A profile form submits only the fields the user touched. Typing the update as Partial makes every field optional at once; a preview card takes Pick . Add a field to Profile and every derived shape follows — no second declaration to forget. Visual Try it interface Profile id: number; name: string; email: string; bio: string; function updateProfile(id: number, patch: Partial ): string const keys = Object.keys(patch).join(","); return "update " + id + ": " + keys; type ProfilePreview = Pick ; const preview: ProfilePreview = name: "sam", bio: "dev" ; console.log(updateProfile(1, name: "jo" )); console.log(preview.name + " - " + preview.bio); type NoBio = Omit ; const short: NoBio = id: 2, name: "al", email: "a@x.com" ; console.log(short.name + " " + short.email); const bad: ProfilePreview = name: "zo", bio: "x", email: "z@x.com" ; console.log(bad.name); Try deleting email from the last object — clean, printing "zo". keyof Profile is the union of its keys, typeof someValue grabs a value's type, and Profile["email"] indexes one field out. Record , Required, and ReturnType round out the daily set — each is one line, each saves a redeclaration. interface Settings theme: string; volume: number; const current: Partial = ; console.log(current); Key takeaways Derive shapes (Partial, Pick, Omit) — never redeclare them. keyof lists keys, typeof borrows a type, indexing reads one field. One source interface keeps forms and payloads in sync. References TypeScript Handbook: utility types. TypeScript Handbook: keyof and indexed access.

title: Why TypeScript exists
description: The late-runtime-error problem, a short verified timeline, and who uses it.
text: JavaScript finds your typos at runtime, in production, in front of users. TypeScript moves that moment earlier: you annotate the shapes you meant, the checker compares every use against them, and wrong code fails in your editor instead of on someone's screen. The problem it solves Dynamic code trusts every caller. A price arrives as the string "12", a refactor renames userName to name in four of five places, and nothing complains until the page renders NaN or crashes. Interviewers love this framing because it is honest: types do not make code correct, they make whole classes of mistakes impossible to ignore. Seen in: Visual Studio Code's core is fully implemented in TypeScript (source code organization, checked 2026); Angular is written in TypeScript and uses it as its primary language (TypeScript Handbook: Angular); the TypeScript compiler itself was self-hosted TypeScript until the 7.0 native port (see the timeline below). A short verified timeline Microsoft unveiled TypeScript 0.8 on October 1, 2012, led by Anders Hejlsberg, as a typed superset of JavaScript for large applications (ten years of TypeScript). TypeScript 1.0 followed in April 2014 with a stability promise for type definition files (announcement). The team announced a native Go port of the compiler in March 2025, and TypeScript 7.0 shipped it on July 8, 2026 — roughly ten times faster, with the typescript package now carrying the native compiler and API consumers staying on the @typescript/typescript6 compatibility package (announcing TypeScript 7.0). The idea in one paragraph Every JavaScript program is already a TypeScript program: add annotations where they pay off, and the compiler erases them on emit. Nothing you write in types survives to runtime — no checks, no overhead, no behavior change. That erasure is the whole deal, and the next page shows exactly where the boundary lies.
